## Testing a twist in the universe's oldest light

Light left over from the early universe may have rotated by a tiny angle during its journey to us. The possible rotation is only about 0.37 degrees, yet confirming it could reveal a physical effect called cosmic birefringence. That would be a sign that empty space treats different orientations of light differently, something the Standard Model of particle physics does not predict.

There is a stubborn problem: a telescope whose polarization detectors are misaligned by the same tiny angle can produce an almost identical signal.

The light in question is the cosmic microwave background, or CMB, released when the universe became transparent about 380,000 years after the big bang. It carries polarization, meaning its electric field has preferred orientations across the sky. Astronomers separate those patterns into E modes, which look radial or ring-like, and B modes, which have a curled structure. A cosmic rotation can convert a little of one pattern into the other.

## Comparing detectors without measuring the cosmic twist

Researchers at UC San Diego developed a calibration test designed to ignore any rotation shared by every map. Instead, it compares detector sets and asks whether their relative angles agree with the calibration pattern inferred by an established method called the Minami-Komatsu analysis.

The team applied the new estimator to eight detector-set maps from the Planck satellite. Those maps create 28 detector-pair comparisons but contain seven independent relative-angle modes. The new reconstruction matched the established calibration pattern with a chi-squared value of 8.18 for seven degrees of freedom, corresponding to a probability-to-exceed of 0.32. None of the individual differences exceeded 1.8 standard deviations, so the analysis found no statistically significant relative calibration inconsistency.

That result matters because the two methods handle foreground emission differently. The agreement suggests that the detector-dependent pattern is present in the polarization data rather than being an artifact of the foreground model used by the established analysis.

## What the result does and does not show

When the researchers conditionally anchored their relative reconstruction to the established method's common calibration, they recovered a rotation of 0.37 plus or minus 0.12 degrees. That agrees with the earlier value.

It is not an independent confirmation of cosmic birefringence. Both reconstructions use the same Planck maps, and the new method deliberately cancels any rotation common to all of them. It therefore cannot establish the absolute angle without an external calibration reference. No sufficiently precise external reference is currently available for Planck.

The method is better understood as an audit of the measurement chain. It rules out one class of relative detector mismatch at useful precision while leaving the central cosmic question open. Future experiments such as the Simons Observatory and LiteBIRD could combine this relative check with dedicated absolute calibration, giving astronomers a cleaner test of whether ancient light truly rotated in transit.

**Measured:** two independent calibration approaches recover consistent relative angles across eight Planck detector maps.

**Inferred:** the possible 0.37-degree cosmic rotation has a stronger calibration foundation, but new physics is not yet confirmed.

### A pulsar's X-ray tail stretches for 42 light-years

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-24_stars_pulsar-xray-tail/
- Published: 2026-09-24
- Topics: [Stars & Stellar Evolution](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/stars-and-stellar-evolution/)
- Freshness context: Published in Science China Physics, Mechanics & Astronomy on 21 September 2026, within the preferred 15-day search window.
- Summary: A faint X-ray tail behind pulsar PSR J1740+1000 reaches about 42 light-years, far beyond the portion seen before. Its alignment with ultrahigh-energy gamma rays suggests that particles can stream in one direction across interstellar space instead of spreading evenly.
- Why it matters: The result gives astronomers a visible trail from a pulsar to gamma rays whose source had been unclear, improving the search for the Milky Way's most powerful natural particle accelerators.
- Suggested next question: How do ordered magnetic fields guide high-energy particles through interstellar space?
- Explore further: [Science China Physics, Mechanics & Astronomy paper](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11433-026-3098-2)
- Sources:
  - [Science China Physics, Mechanics & Astronomy: Anisotropic particle transport from a pulsar wind nebula revealed by Einstein Probe and LHAASO](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11433-026-3098-2)
  - [Chinese Academy of Sciences: Einstein Probe and LHAASO reveal a 42-light-year directed journey of cosmic rays](https://english.cas.cn/newsroom/research-news/202609/t20260917_1200807.shtml)

Fuller note:

## A particle trail longer than a star neighborhood

A faint X-ray streak behind a dead star has turned out to be about 42 light-years long. The streak begins near PSR J1740+1000, a pulsar roughly 4,600 light-years from Earth, and points toward a patch of ultrahigh-energy gamma rays previously lacking an obvious source.

A pulsar is the compact, rapidly rotating core left after a massive star explodes. Its magnetic field can drive a wind of electrons and other charged particles moving close to the speed of light. Where those particles travel, they can leave radiation that telescopes detect even though the particles themselves are invisible.

Earlier observations by XMM-Newton had revealed only a several-light-year section of this pulsar's tail. China's Einstein Probe changed the scale of the picture. Its Follow-up X-ray Telescope combines a wide field of view with a low instrumental background, useful for finding large, dim structures. During about 70,000 seconds of observation, it traced the tail across roughly 32 arcminutes of sky. At the pulsar's estimated distance, that angle corresponds to about 42 light-years, making this the longest X-ray tail yet detected from a pulsar wind nebula.

## Two kinds of light, one particle population

The geometry alone is suggestive. The X-ray tail extends in the same direction as ultrahigh-energy gamma-ray emission measured by the ground-based Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory, or LHAASO. The researchers also found that the energy patterns of the X-rays and gamma rays can be produced by the same population of energetic electrons.

Those electrons emit X-rays as they curve through magnetic fields, a process called synchrotron radiation. They can also collide with low-energy photons and transfer enough energy to turn them into gamma rays. Seeing both signals along the same route gives astronomers a way to follow the particles from their likely accelerator near the pulsar into surrounding space.

This matters because cosmic particles are often expected to scatter off irregular magnetic fields and spread in many directions. Here, the trail remains narrow across tens of light-years. The result suggests that particle transport can be strongly directional, which may explain why some gamma-ray sources appear offset from the object that created their particles. The brightest gamma-ray location need not mark the accelerator itself.

## What remains uncertain

The observations establish the long X-ray structure and its close match to the gamma-ray emission. The explanation for its shape is still an inference. One possibility is that an orderly interstellar magnetic field acts like a track, allowing particles to move easily along it while limiting sideways motion. Another is a narrow, continuing outflow that carries particles outward like water through a hose.

The present measurements do not distinguish between those mechanisms. Further observations of the tail's motion, spectrum, and magnetic environment could show whether the route is set mainly by the surrounding field or by the pulsar's own outflow.

**Measured:** a roughly 42-light-year X-ray tail, aligned spatially and spectrally with ultrahigh-energy gamma-ray emission.

**Inferred:** both signals trace the same high-energy particles traveling preferentially away from PSR J1740+1000.

### Rubin finds seven almost-dark galaxies near Virgo's M49

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-23_galaxies_rubin-almost-dark-virgo/
- Published: 2026-09-23
- Topics: [Galaxies & Galactic Evolution](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/galaxies-and-galactic-evolution/)
- Freshness context: Posted to arXiv as 2609.19246 on 16 September 2026, inside the preferred 15-day freshness window for this daily note.
- Summary: In Rubin LSST Data Preview 2, a team led by Minh Ngoc Le reports seven almost-dark galaxies around M49 in the Virgo Cluster. Their g-band central surface brightnesses run from about 26.9 to 28.5 mag per square arcsecond, with half-light radii of about 0.6 to 4.6 kpc and stellar masses near 10^6 to 10^7 solar masses.
- Why it matters: Galaxies this faint were known mainly in the Local Group. Finding a population at Virgo distance shows Rubin can catch them systematically, which is the path to counting how many exist and testing dark-matter models at the faint end of the luminosity function.
- Suggested next question: How surface brightness, half-light radius, and stellar mass place a galaxy among ultra-diffuse and almost-dark populations.
- Explore further: [arXiv: Rubin LSST DP2 unveils almost-dark galaxies in the Virgo Cluster](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19246)
- Sources:
  - [arXiv: Rubin LSST DP2 unveils almost-dark galaxies in the Virgo Cluster (2609.19246)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19246)
  - [arXiv HTML full text: Rubin LSST DP2 unveils almost-dark galaxies in the Virgo Cluster](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.19246)

Fuller note:

## Galaxies you almost cannot see

Most galaxy catalogs stop where the light gets thin. A spiral or elliptical with a bright core is easy. A diffuse patch that never rises much above the night sky is not. Astronomers call the faintest of those patches almost-dark galaxies. They are not empty. They are just extremely dilute in starlight.

Until recently, the clearest examples lived in the Local Group, where proximity lets surveys catch stars that would vanish at greater distance. Analogues should exist farther out. Catching them needs imaging that goes deep enough across a wide field. That is the job Rubin was built for.

## Seven patches around M49

A team led by Minh Ngoc Le at the Instituto de Astrofisica de Canarias, with Johan H. Knapen, Zeljko Ivezic, and a large Rubin collaboration, searched Data Preview 2 of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time. The paper, "Rubin LSST DP2 unveils almost-dark galaxies in the Virgo Cluster," went onto arXiv on 16 September 2026 as 2609.19246.

Their hunt centered on the Cosmic Treasure Chest field near M49, the giant elliptical that anchors the Virgo B subcluster. That field spans about 24 square degrees. In the g, r, and i bands the coadds reach surface-brightness limits near the depth expected for the full 10-year survey. Visual inspection turned up seven candidates. The authors label them AD 1 through AD 7, with coordinates such as Rubin J122848.6+085727 for AD 1 and Rubin J122703.1+080018 for AD 7.

Measured at an adopted Virgo distance of about 16.17 Mpc, the seven objects show g-band central surface brightnesses from about 26.9 to 28.5 mag per square arcsecond. Half-light radii run from about 0.6 to 4.6 kpc. Stellar masses sit near 10^6 to 10^7 solar masses. Most have flat Sersic profiles with index below 1. Mean colors near (g-r) of 0.5 point to old, metal-poor stars. None show clear tidal shredding in the images the team presents.

## Why "almost dark" is not the same as ultra-diffuse

Ultra-diffuse galaxies can be large and faint. Almost-dark galaxies sit even fainter, often by a factor of tens in surface brightness at similar size. The seven Virgo finds land among the faintest dwarfs known, closer in properties to Local Group satellites such as Andromeda XXI, XXIII, and XXV than to classic Coma ultra-diffuse galaxies.

AD 7 is the standout. Its half-light radius is about 4.6 kpc, and its central g-band surface brightness is about 28.5 mag per square arcsecond. A single Sersic fit fails, so the team used a core-Sersic model. If the object is real and at Virgo distance, it is among the most extreme low-surface-brightness systems reported in that cluster. The authors flag that AD 7 sits near bright neighbors in a region that may be oversubtracted, and they call for follow-up with a low-surface-brightness-friendly strategy before anyone treats it as settled.

## Distance, gas, and what is still open

Association with Virgo rests on projected distance from M49 (mostly within about 1 Mpc of its virial radius) and on the angular sizes. Push the same objects to twice Virgo's distance and their physical sizes become extreme relative to formation models. Pull them into the foreground near 5 Mpc and individual stars should start to resolve at Rubin's depth. The images stay smooth. That sandwich of arguments favors Virgo membership, with AD 4 near the edge of the virial radius.

ALFALFA gives no HI detection for any of the seven, with an upper limit near 10^7 solar masses at Virgo distance. Except for AD 4, which lies outside the VESTIGE footprint, none show H-alpha either. Red, quiet, and gas-poor is the picture. Background subtraction in DP2 can still clip faint outskirts, so total light and profile shapes may be underestimated. Formal fit errors also understate sky and PSF systematics. Those caveats belong next to the census claim, not after it.

## What Rubin's early data already proves

This is a proof of concept, not a complete catalog of the field. Several of the objects were missed by earlier deep Virgo surveys. One (AD 5) was found independently by another group. Three appear in a recent NGVS catalog as well. The useful sentence is simpler: early Rubin coadds already reach the almost-dark regime outside the Local Group.

The full 10-year LSST will cover about 18,000 square degrees at similar or greater depth. A statistical sample of almost-dark galaxies is what theorists need when they compare the faint end of the luminosity function to warm versus cold dark-matter predictions. Seven objects do not settle that debate. They show the survey can collect the objects the debate needs.

Measured: seven low-surface-brightness candidates around M49 in Rubin DP2, with the sizes, brightnesses, and masses above. Inferred: a Virgo population of Local-Group-like almost-dark galaxies is now reachable in wide-field optical data, and AD 7 is the extreme case that most needs confirmation.

### Radio bursts pin a magnetic field on Beta Pictoris b

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-22_exoplanets_beta-pic-b-radio-field/
- Published: 2026-09-22
- Topics: [Exoplanets](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/exoplanets/)
- Freshness context: Posted to arXiv as 2609.16720 in September 2026, inside the preferred 15-day freshness window for this daily note.
- Summary: MeerKAT has localized auroral radio bursts to the giant planet Beta Pictoris b, about 20 parsecs away. The emission reaches 3.5 GHz and implies a magnetic field of at least about 1.25 kilogauss, the first direct field-strength measurement for an exoplanet.
- Why it matters: Magnetic fields shape how planets hold atmospheres and how they interact with stellar winds, yet none had been measured directly beyond the Solar System. A confirmed exoplanet with a radio-derived field turns a long-standing model target into an observable, and it opens a path to map fields on other nearby imaged giants.
- Suggested next question: How electron cyclotron maser emission turns the highest radio frequency into a lower limit on a planet's magnetic field strength.
- Explore further: [arXiv: Discovery of radio emission from the exoplanet Beta Pictoris b](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16720)
- Sources:
  - [arXiv: Discovery of radio emission from the exoplanet Beta Pictoris b (2609.16720)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16720)
  - [arXiv HTML full text: Discovery of radio emission from the exoplanet Beta Pictoris b](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.16720v1)

Fuller note:

## A magnetic field you can hear

Planetary magnetic fields matter. They steer atmospheric escape, shape how a planet meets a stellar wind, and leave clues about the metal and rock deep inside. Until now, nobody had measured one directly for a planet beyond the Solar System. Models filled the gap. Direct numbers did not.

The clean signal is auroral radio, the same kind of emission Jupiter and Earth produce when energetic electrons spiral along magnetic field lines. The highest frequency of that emission tracks the field strength at the source. Radio astronomers have caught similar bursts from ultracool dwarfs, and earlier searches of planet-hosting systems either found nothing or could not tell whether the star or the planet was talking. That ambiguity is the problem this result breaks.

## MeerKAT points at Beta Pictoris b

A team led by K. N. Ortiz Ceballos at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, with E. Berger and Y. Cendes, observed the Beta Pictoris system with South Africa's MeerKAT array on four dates in 2025 and 2026, in the L and S bands between about 0.85 and 3.5 GHz. Beta Pictoris sits about 20 parsecs away. The star is roughly 23 million years old, magnetically quiet, and hosts a debris disk plus at least three giant planets. The most massive, Beta Pictoris b, weighs about 12 Jupiter masses and orbits near 10 astronomical units. At its widest, the planet sits about half an arcsecond from the star, far enough for careful radio imaging to separate the two.

They detect a radio source in every epoch. The hard part is ownership. After tying the radio frame to Gaia using nine quasars and one VLBI calibrator, and folding in tests for ionospheric refraction and fitting error, the corrected position matches planet b and conflicts with the host star at about 4.4 sigma and with planet c at about 4.8 sigma. Measured: the radio spot sits on the planet, not the star.

## Bursts that give a field strength

The emission is not a steady hum. It comes as rapid, recurring bursts with circular polarization of about 40 to 70 percent, plus fainter emission between bursts. The polarization and the short timescales point to electron cyclotron maser radiation. Plasma emission would need densities the team finds implausible for a planetary magnetosphere. The S-band burst reaches 3.5 GHz, the top of that observing band, and is also the most polarized. Under the cyclotron-frequency rule, that ceiling requires a magnetic field of at least about 1.25 kilogauss at the emission site. That is the first direct field-strength measurement for an exoplanet. It also sits above the host star's known dipole upper limit of roughly 0.3 kilogauss, another reason the star cannot be the source.

The authors favor magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling, the same rotationally driven engine that powers aurorae at Jupiter and at many ultracool dwarfs. Beta Pictoris b spins in about 8 to 9 hours. An about 8-hour gap between two L-band bursts sits near that period and may be rotational modulation. Stellar-wind driving and an Io-like moon interaction both under-predict the observed power in their checks. Those alternatives are disfavored, not merely left open as equals.

## Why the number travels

Because Beta Pictoris b has a dynamically measured mass, the radio field can be set beside dynamo scaling laws calibrated on Solar System planets and low-mass stars. The planet lands where those laws predict a young, massive giant should sit. Continued monitoring can map magnetic geometry. Seven more nearby directly imaged giants sit at separations where the same localization trick can work, once radio arrays gain about five to seven times more sensitivity.

Caveats belong in the open. The result rests on four observing blocks and on frame-tie systematics that the team inflate on purpose. The paper is an arXiv preprint (2609.16720), so peer review is still ahead. The 1.25 kilogauss figure is a lower limit set by the highest detected frequency, not a full map of the field. Measured: auroral radio, localized to Beta Pictoris b, with a cyclotron ceiling that implies at least about 1.25 kilogauss. Inferred: a working planetary dynamo on a confirmed exoplanet, finally caught in radio light.

### Black holes big and small may launch jets by the same rule

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-21_black-holes_universal-jet-rule/
- Published: 2026-09-21
- Topics: [Black Holes](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/black-holes/)
- Freshness context: Published in Nature Astronomy on 17 September 2026, within the preferred 15-day freshness window.
- Summary: A study of stars torn apart by giant black holes finds jets switching on at two points in the feeding cycle: once at very high rates, and again near 2 percent of the Eddington limit. Stellar-mass black holes in the Milky Way already change state near that same 2 percent mark.
- Why it matters: Stellar-mass black holes finish a feeding cycle in days or weeks. A typical supermassive black hole changes over thousands of years. Tidal disruptions shrink that wait to years. A shared accretion-rate switch, if it holds, turns irregular radio flares into something observers can schedule, with real gaps still in the sample.
- Suggested next question: How a tidal disruption, a star torn apart by a giant black hole, lets astronomers watch a feeding cycle that would otherwise take thousands of years.
- Explore further: [Nature Astronomy: A universal critical accretion rate for black hole jet formation](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-026-02951-1)
- Sources:
  - [Nature Astronomy: A universal critical accretion rate for black hole jet formation](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-026-02951-1)
  - [Institute for Advanced Study: IAS Scholar Reveals Universal Rule of Black Hole Burps](https://www.ias.edu/news/ias-scholar-reveals-universal-rule-black-hole-burps)

Fuller note:

## The slow ones were hard to watch

A feeding black hole does not keep everything it pulls in. Some of the gas comes back out as a jet: narrow, fast, bright in the radio, and, over a long enough time, a way to shove gas around in the host galaxy. The suspicion, for years, was that the on-switch looks the same for a stellar-mass black hole and for a supermassive one. Scale the feeding rate properly, and the physics of accretion does not know the mass. Testing that hunch has been the annoying part.

Stellar-mass black holes in the Milky Way swing through a feeding cycle in days or weeks. You can watch a jet turn on. A typical supermassive black hole in an active galaxy changes over thousands of years. No program sits with one of those systems long enough to see it cross a threshold. The comparison stalled on that mismatch of clocks. A rule that might be universal was stuck looking untestable at the top end of the mass range.

## A torn star as a shorter film

A Nature Astronomy paper by Adelle Goodwin, of Curtin University's International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research, and Andrew Mummery, of the Institute for Advanced Study, uses tidal disruptions to get a shorter film. A tidal disruption happens when a star passes too close to a giant black hole and the black hole's gravity tears the star apart. The debris forms a compact disk that can evolve in years rather than millennia. A human career is suddenly long enough to watch the meal.

They assembled optical, ultraviolet, X-ray, and radio data for twenty such events, from telescopes in America, Australia, India, South Africa, and in space. For ten of the twenty, the feeding rate and the timing of the radio outflow could both be modeled well enough to ask a sharp question. At what point in the meal does the jet start? The Institute for Advanced Study's note on Mummery's side of the work calls the pattern a universal rule of black hole burps. The measurement under the joke is the accretion rate at launch.

## Two moments, one of them familiar

The ten events show two launching phases. The first is early, while the black hole is feeding at super-Eddington rates. The Eddington limit is the feeding rate at which outward radiation pressure would balance the black hole's gravity. Super-Eddington means more inflow than that balance. The second launch comes later, hundreds to thousands of days after the disruption, when the feeding rate has fallen to about two percent of the Eddington limit.

The two-percent mark is the result that travels. Stellar-mass black holes in the Milky Way already change state and launch a compact jet near that same fraction. In the disruption sample, the delayed radio flares cluster around it. The prompt flares cluster at or above the Eddington rate. Goodwin and Mummery argue that one scale-invariant process covers both, across a huge range of black-hole mass. That argument is the interpretation. The clustering of the flares at those two rates is the measurement, and it rests on ten events, not on twenty.

The same split accounts for a known nuisance. Some disruptions launch a jet almost at once. Others go quiet for months or years and then flare in the radio. Those can be one feeding curve, sampled at different times, rather than two species of black hole. Miss the early window, while the rate is still at or above Eddington, and the source looks silent until it crosses about two percent of Eddington.

## A forecast, with the holes left visible

If the shared switch is real, a jet launch has a preferred accretion rate, and observers can aim scarce telescopes, the Square Kilometre Array among them, at the moment the rate is due to cross it. The paper's population check is consistent with that picture. Quote it as a check, not as a new survey. Only a minority of these disks are expected to go super-Eddington, which lines up with prompt-radio detections of roughly 30 to 50 percent. About 40 percent are expected to pass the two-percent threshold inside an observable window of a few years, close to independent estimates of how often the delayed flares appear.

The holes are part of the result, not a footnote to skip. Ten events had data good enough to time both the disk and the outflow. Twenty were assembled, and half of them did not make that cut. Strongly jetted, relativistic disruptions were left out, because the jet swamps the disk and the feeding rate cannot be measured the same way. The disk model is less trustworthy in the super-Eddington regime. The authors note that this uncertainty would tend to under-predict the feeding rate there, which would not erase the prompt, high-rate group. It does mean the early, super-Eddington launches are the softer of the two clusters. Launch dates assume a roughly constant outflow speed. Compact jets add more uncertainty on top of that.

The claim to keep is a shared accretion-rate threshold, supported in ten well-modeled disruptions and matching a threshold already used for stellar-mass black holes. It is not a promise that every quiet nucleus will fire on schedule. Measured: radio outflows in those ten events line up with two feeding stages, one at or above the Eddington limit and one near two percent of it, hundreds to thousands of days later. Inferred: the same scale-free switch runs from stellar remnants to supermassive black holes. The next watch is more disruptions, followed as they fade, to see whether the late radio outburst keeps arriving at that two-percent crossing.

### Supernova bubbles may keep Andromeda's gas in motion

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-20_galaxies_andromeda-supernova-turbulence/
- Published: 2026-09-20
- Topics: [Galaxies & Galactic Evolution](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/galaxies-and-galactic-evolution/)
- Freshness context: Published in Nature Astronomy on 17 September 2026, within the preferred 15-day freshness window.
- Summary: Using China's FAST radio telescope and the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array, a Tsinghua-led team mapped 118 expanding superbubbles in Andromeda. The energy those bubbles deliver lines up with the energy needed to keep the galaxy's neutral hydrogen turbulent, in magnitude and across the disk.
- Why it matters: Turbulence in galactic gas keeps losing energy, and something has to supply it or star-forming clouds would settle. Andromeda now has a counted population of superbubbles whose input matches that loss, in size and in how both change with distance from the center. Clustered supernovae are the driver the team names.
- Suggested next question: How winds and repeated supernovae from a group of massive stars blow a superbubble and leave turbulent gas behind.
- Explore further: [Nature Astronomy: Supernova origin of galactic turbulence revealed by superbubbles](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-026-02981-9)
- Sources:
  - [Nature Astronomy: Supernova origin of galactic turbulence revealed by superbubbles](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-026-02981-9)
  - [Tsinghua University: Superbubbles drive turbulence in the Andromeda galaxy](https://astro.tsinghua.edu.cn/en/info/1026/2866.htm)

Fuller note:

## A problem posed in 1979

In 1979, Carl Heiles found giant shells of neutral hydrogen in the Milky Way. Neutral hydrogen, often called HI, is cold atomic hydrogen gas, the kind radio telescopes map. Some of those shells span hundreds or thousands of light-years. The largest one required more energy than a single supernova could supply. Structures like that are called superbubbles. A superbubble is a giant cavity blown when stellar winds and repeated supernova explosions from a group of massive stars sweep the surrounding gas into a shell.

The same objects brush against a second, older question. What keeps turbulence going? Turbulence here means irregular gas motions on many scales, the kind that help decide how fast clouds collapse into stars. Those motions continuously lose energy. The fraction of supernova energy that actually reaches the gas has been hard to pin down, so it has been easy to assume an efficiency and hard to measure one. A team led by Professor Di Li at Tsinghua University used superbubbles in the Andromeda galaxy to replace that assumption with a number taken from the gas itself.

## 118 shells, weighed from the gas

Andromeda, also called M31, lies about 2.5 million light-years away. That distance is a gift. We see the whole disk from outside, which is a view we cannot have of the Milky Way from the inside. The team combined China's FAST radio telescope with the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array in the United States. FAST is sensitive to the diffuse gas. The VLA picks up the fine structure of the shells. Together they show both.

The map contains 118 expanding superbubbles. Some expand slowly, with estimated ages up to 40 million years. An old, slow shell still counts. Turbulence has to be driven for a long time, not in a single blast, and a bubble that has been growing for tens of millions of years is a record of prolonged energy input.

The observations supplied three quantities for the shells: size, expansion speed, and the density of the gas around them. From those, the team estimated the kinetic energy transferred into the gas and how long the input lasted. Divide energy by time and you have an average rate. That rate is the replacement for an assumed transfer efficiency. It is estimated from the bubbles and their surroundings, not inserted by hand so that a model will balance.

The paper, "Supernova origin of galactic turbulence revealed by superbubbles," was published online in Nature Astronomy on 17 September 2026. Di Li's group in Tsinghua's Department of Astronomy led the work, with the National Astronomical Observatories of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and international collaborators. Tsinghua is the first-listed affiliation. Fanyi Meng of Tsinghua and Chao-Wei Tsai and Jingwen Wu of the National Astronomical Observatories share first authorship. Di Li is the corresponding author.

## The rates agree, in size and across the disk

The team also estimated how quickly the turbulence loses energy, taking galactic rotation and thermal motions into account. The input rate from the superbubbles and the loss rate of the turbulence agree in magnitude. They also agree in how they vary with distance from the galaxy's center. A match that is only a single galaxy-wide total could be a coincidence of averages. A match that follows the same trend from the inner disk to the outer disk is harder to wave off.

This is the sense in which the energy in the bubbles closely matches the energy needed to sustain the galaxy's turbulence. Tsinghua compares rates, injection against dissipation, and the agreement is in magnitude and in the trend with radius. No percentage is stated, and none is added here. Their figure marks injection rates, a band for turbulent losses, an estimated contribution from the magnetorotational instability (rotation plus magnetic fields), and an earlier bubble sample. Another driver is on the plot. The text's claim is that clustered supernovae can maintain M31's neutral-hydrogen turbulence.

"Can maintain" is a sufficiency claim about the neutral hydrogen. It is not a claim that every other driver contributes zero, and the figure's extra shading is a reminder of that. It is also not a claim about every phase of the gas. The turbulence in question is the turbulence in the atomic hydrogen. Molecular clouds and hot halo gas are a different measurement.

## What was counted, and what the driver claim adds

Counted: 118 expanding superbubbles, their sizes, their speeds, the densities around them, and ages up to about 40 million years for the slow ones. Derived from those counts: kinetic energy, duration, and an average power delivered to the gas, plus a separate estimate of how fast turbulence drains. Inferred: successive supernovae, collected into superbubbles, supply enough energy to sustain the observed neutral-hydrogen turbulence in Andromeda. The paper's title is stronger than "contribute." It says the supernova origin is revealed. The evidence offered for that sentence is the rate comparison, including the shared trend with radius.

Heiles's largest shells already showed that one explosion underfills the biggest cavities. A group of massive stars pours wind into the same volume and then explodes over millions of years. The cavities merge into a superbubble. In Andromeda, 118 of them can be added up, and the motion they leave is a galactic energy budget rather than a local scar.

Later stars form from the gas those explosions stirred, so the budget reaches the next generation. Andromeda is one resolvable spiral, not a stand-in for every galaxy. The scope is this map and this galaxy's neutral hydrogen.

Tsinghua's note is the group's summary. Nature Astronomy is the authority for the fits and the other drivers. Groups of exploding stars have inflated 118 giant bubbles in Andromeda's atomic gas, and the power in those bubbles lines up with the power the turbulence requires.

### The Solar System sorted its building blocks from the start

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-19_solar-system_planetesimal-sorting/
- Published: 2026-09-19
- Topics: [Solar System & Planetary Science](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/solar-system-and-planetary-science/); [Planet Formation](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/planet-formation/)
- Freshness context: Published in Nature Astronomy on 18 September 2026, within the preferred 15-day freshness window.
- Summary: Meteorite chemistry, reported in a Nature Astronomy paper dated 18 September 2026, says the Solar System sorted its raw materials within the first million years. The earliest small bodies were already rich in heat-processed rocky beads and held much less fine, ice-rich dust than bodies that formed later.
- Why it matters: Planet formation was not a matter of scooping whatever dust happened to be nearby. If the first planetesimals were already a sorted mix, hot rock and icy dust were being separated as those small bodies formed. Later planets, moons, and asteroids inherited a pantry that was divided from the start.
- Suggested next question: How gas drag in a young star's disk can sort dust and rocky beads before they gather into planetesimals.
- Explore further: [Nature Astronomy: Planetesimal compositions governed by aerodynamic sorting from the onset of Solar System formation](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-026-02976-6)
- Sources:
  - [Nature Astronomy: Planetesimal compositions governed by aerodynamic sorting from the onset of Solar System formation](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-026-02976-6)
  - [Yale University / Phys.org: From the start, the solar system chose fire over ice to build its first bodies](https://phys.org/news/2026-09-solar-chose-ice-bodies.html)

Fuller note:

## Meteorites that are not a random scoop

A planetesimal is an early small world, built from dust and rock, that can later feed a planet or shatter into the meteorites that reach Earth. A Nature Astronomy paper published on 18 September 2026 reads the chemistry of those meteorites as a sorting record. Within the Solar System's first million years, the material that built the earliest of these bodies was already being separated. Those first bodies held unusually large amounts of heat-processed rocky beads and much less fine, ice-rich dust than bodies that formed later.

The beads are chondrules: millimeter-scale droplets of melted rock that cooled quickly and were later glued into larger stones. "Heat-processed" means the melting happened before the planetesimal assembled. The fine dust is the other ingredient, colder, often carrying ice and grains that never melted. A body built from an excess of chondrules and a deficit of that dust did not form from a random scoop of the disk. Something had already divided the pantry.

That division is the result people will quote. It is a statement about composition and about time. The earliest small worlds were not a well-mixed average of everything the young Sun's disk contained. They were a selected sample, tilted toward rock that had already been melted, and away from the fine icy dust that shows up more strongly later. Yale's account of the paper, republished by Phys.org, frames the same result as the early Solar System choosing fire over ice for its first bodies. The frame is vivid. The measurement under it is the meteorite mix and the clock that puts the mix inside the first million years.

## Drag as the favored sorter

The paper's title names the mechanism the authors favor: aerodynamic sorting, operating from the onset of Solar System formation. In a disk that is mostly gas, solids of different sizes feel drag differently. Small dust stays coupled to the gas and rides along with it. Larger beads drift relative to the gas, concentrate, and can be gathered into clumps while the fines are left behind or arrive later. A clump gathered that way is born already chondrule-rich. It does not have to wait for a planet to sort the ingredients after the fact.

Drag itself is a standard process in a gas disk. Applying it as the governor of these particular meteorite groups is the authors' step. The title states that step as the claim. A reader who wants the chemical argument, the meteorite groups, and the timing method belongs in the Nature Astronomy article. The public summary supports the ingredients, the first-million-year window, and aerodynamic sorting as the favored explanation. It does not, in the account used here, walk through isotope ratios or name a percentage of chondrules. Those details stay in the paper.

Other ways to concentrate melted beads exist. The authors are arguing that aerodynamic sorting fits the early, chondrule-rich, dust-poor pattern. "Fits" is an interpretation laid on top of a chemical measurement. Keep the two in different hands. The meteorites record what the first bodies contained. The drag law is the story offered for how the disk assembled that mix and skipped the fines.

## Why the first million years changes the story

"Within the first million years" is early even on the clock of the disk. The gas disk around the young Sun lasts a few million years. If the first planetesimals are already a sorted, chondrule-rich population at the one-million-year mark, planet formation did not begin with a well-mixed sludge that only later got organized. The separation of materials is part of the birth of the small bodies. It is not a cleanup that waited until planets existed and then rearranged their leftovers.

Later bodies, with more of the fine ice-rich dust, then sample a disk that had changed, or a region the early sorting did not empty. The sequence matters for anyone reconstructing raw materials. A meteorite from an early planetesimal is not a fair stand-in for "what the Solar System was made of" in bulk. It is a stand-in for what could be gathered, at that moment, from the particle sizes the gas was willing to concentrate. Use it as a bulk recipe and you will over-weight the melted rock and under-weight the ice.

It is tempting to draw a line from that early contrast to dry inner asteroids and icy outer bodies. The rhyme is not a proof, and this paper is not a new map of every asteroid class. The claim is about the earliest small worlds, and about compositions aerodynamic sorting can impose from the start. Planets and moons inherit that mix later. The measurement is the first mix.

## Measurement on one side, mechanism on the other

Measured, via meteorite chemistry: early planetesimals unusually rich in once-molten rocky beads, poorer in fine icy dust than later bodies, inside the first million years. Interpreted: gas drag sorted particle sizes from the outset and governed those compositions. Drag is already known to move big grains and small grains differently. A different concentrator that also prefers chondrules could be asked to fit the same meteorites. The paper's case is that aerodynamic sorting does the governing.

Phys.org is a secondary write-up of the Yale account, not a second set of laboratory measurements. Nature Astronomy is the authority for the chemistry and the timing. In ordinary language, particle size decides how tightly a grain is tied to the gas, and the gas is most of the disk. The first rocks are built from beads the gas has already sorted, including beads melted before they were assembled. Fire, in the Yale headline, is that earlier melting. Ice is the fine dust the earliest bodies largely missed.

### The youngest known planet is still forming in its disk

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-18_exoplanets_elias-2-24-b-youngest-planet/
- Published: 2026-09-18
- Topics: [Exoplanets](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/exoplanets/); [Planet Formation](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/planet-formation/)
- Freshness context: Published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters on 16 September 2026, within the preferred 15-day freshness window.
- Summary: Astronomers have confirmed Elias 2-24 b, a planet about Jupiter's mass and less than a million years old, still inside the disk around its star, 450 light-years away. It is the youngest known planet. The previous record holders, four worlds at PDS 70 and WISPIT 2, are all more than 5 million years old.
- Why it matters: Models already had trouble building a Jupiter in about 5 million years at Jupiter's distance, and they need still longer farther out. Elias 2-24 b is younger than a million years, already about Jupiter's mass, and 55 times Earth's orbital distance from its star. The growth clock in the models is missing something.
- Suggested next question: How giant planets grow inside disks of gas and dust, and why a gap in that disk can mark a planet that is still forming.
- Explore further: [NASA Science: Confirmed planet Elias 2-24 b is the youngest known world](https://science.nasa.gov/universe/newfound-baby-planet-smashes-record-for-youngest-known-world/)
- Sources:
  - [NASA Science: Confirmed planet Elias 2-24 b is the youngest known world](https://science.nasa.gov/universe/newfound-baby-planet-smashes-record-for-youngest-known-world/)
  - [The Astrophysical Journal Letters: study published 16 September 2026](https://iopscience.iop.org/journal/2041-8205)

Fuller note:

## A confirmed planet still in its disk

Elias 2-24 b is a confirmed planet about as massive as Jupiter, less than a million years old, and still inside the natal disk of dust and gas around its star. NASA calls it the youngest known planet. The star lies about 450 light-years from Earth. The paper, led by Andrea Bernardi, a doctoral candidate at Universidad Diego Portales in Chile, was published on 16 September 2026 in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. NASA's science page, last updated 17 September 2026, is the public account. The journal link attached here points at the Letters homepage, not at an article DOI. The specific paper is the one NASA cites.

"Confirmed" is the word that had to be earned. About a decade ago, ALMA, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array in Chile, showed a gap in the star's dusty disk. The European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope then picked up a faint point of light sitting in that gap. A point of light in a disk can be a planet. It can also be a clump, a background star, or a defect in the image. The argument sat there for years.

Bernardi's team used archival coronagraph observations of seven stars at the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii, which partners with NASA under a cooperative agreement. A coronagraph blocks the star's glare so fainter nearby light can be recorded. Each star has a disk of dust, gas, and chunks of ice and rock, with gaps that hint at planets. NASA calls those disks debris disks, and also calls Elias 2-24 b's surroundings a natal disk that still holds dust and gas. The gas is the reservoir a world still gaining mass would draw on.

## Why the age breaks the schedule

The previous record holders were a four-way tie: two planets at the star PDS 70 and two at WISPIT 2. All four are more than 5 million years old. Lucas Cieza, a professor at the Instituto de Estudios Astrofísicos in Chile and a co-author, says planet-formation models already struggled with worlds that old. Elias 2-24 b, he argues, shows that even the best of those models still miss some processes. That is a statement about the models. The planet itself is not missing. It is in the gap.

The timing problem is concrete. Current models predict that a Jupiter-mass planet at Jupiter's distance from its star takes about 5 million years to form. Jupiter's distance is just over five times the Earth-Sun distance. Farther out, the models need still longer. The point of light in this disk sits 55 times farther from its star than Earth is from the Sun, and the system is younger than a million years. On the standard clock, the gap is too early and the orbit is too wide for a Jupiter to be there already.

Most of the roughly 6,000 confirmed exoplanets, planets orbiting other stars, are billions of years old and sit close to their stars. An overwhelming majority were found by transits, when a planet crosses its star and the light dips. Transits are hard to catch when a planet is buried in dust or orbits far out, so models of giant-planet growth have leaned on theory and on disks where planets cannot yet be seen. Cieza's other point is that gap in the census. Stars and planets keep forming, so every stage exists somewhere, and most telescopes are still largely blind to planets this young.

## A decade of arguing about one point of light

Bernardi expected the planets to sit inside the gaps, because the planets are what carve them. Elias 2-24 b sits in a gap. The location matches the expectation. The motion is what turned the candidate into a confirmation.

The Keck Observatory Archive, a NASA-funded partnership with the NASA Exoplanet Science Institute at Caltech/IPAC, has the same point in observations from 2018 and 2020. Over those two years it moved like a planet, not like a background star or an imaging defect. Bernardi says the object sits at the limit of current telescopes, and that the confirmation needed ALMA, the Very Large Telescope, and Keck together.

Measured: a gap, a faint source inside it, a Jupiter-like mass, an age under a million years, a separation of 55 Earth-Sun distances, and a shift between 2018 and 2020 consistent with an orbit. Inferred: the planet is carving the gap, and it is still gaining mass because the disk is still there. Nobody watched a stream of gas fall onto it in a single night. Whether the mass arrived by a collapsing disk fragment or by a core that then pulled in gas is not settled in NASA's account, and it is not assigned here.

## What Roman changes, and what it does not

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope launched on 30 August 2026 with a more powerful coronagraph. Used the same way, it could reach planets on much smaller orbits, including Jupiter analogs now lost in the glare. Elias 2-24 b orbits about 10 times farther out than those analogs. Bernardi's practical point is that detections like this one should get easier. It is not a template for the closer giants Roman is built to chase.

One disk is not a photocopy of the young Solar System. What it does show is a giant planet that already has about Jupiter's mass before a million years have passed, far from its star, inside a gap, while gas is still present.

The article is the one NASA cites, published 16 September 2026 in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. The link on file is the journal homepage, so no DOI is stated here. The record to keep is the age, the mass, the distance from the star, and a motion that survived the checks against a background star or an image defect.

### A simulation grows early black holes from heavy seeds

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-17_black-holes_little-red-dots-heavy-seeds/
- Published: 2026-09-17
- Topics: [Black Holes](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/black-holes/); [Cosmology & Early Universe](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/cosmology-and-early-universe/)
- Freshness context: Published in Nature on 16 September 2026, within the preferred 15-day freshness window.
- Summary: Webb keeps finding giant black holes, and compact red sources called little red dots, at times when a stellar-mass seed growing at a modest rate should not yet be huge. A Nature simulation grows heavy seeds from unusually massive first stars, lets them feed furiously for a short time, and produces objects that look like those dots.
- Why it matters: The early black holes are an observational problem: they look too big, too soon. This paper is a simulation, not a detection of the first stars. It shows one route by which heavy seeds in dense gas can front-load their growth and leave compact red sources, if the massive stars at the start are granted.
- Suggested next question: Little red dots: compact, reddish sources Webb found that may be an early, dust-hidden stage of supermassive black hole growth.
- Explore further: [Nature: Overmassive black holes and little red dots naturally form in simulations](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-10985-8)
- Sources:
  - [Nature](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-10985-8)

Fuller note:

## Too big, too soon

Giant black holes show up early. Webb finds them, and finds the compact red sources called little red dots, at times when a black hole that started near the mass of a star and then ate at a polite rate should not yet be enormous. A Nature paper published on 16 September 2026 reports a simulation in which the early universe grows those objects anyway. The route is short. Unusually massive first stars collapse into large black-hole seeds. Those seeds then grow extremely quickly for a brief time. The output looks like the little red dots.

The title's word for the black holes is "overmassive," meaning too heavy for how little time the young universe had given them. The title also says the overmassive black holes and the little red dots form naturally in the simulations. "Naturally" is the authors' claim that the dots and the heavy black holes come out of the run, rather than being painted on at the end. The seeds and the dense gas are the setup. The quick growth and the compact red appearance are what the run produces.

The method matters more than the headline. This is a simulation. It is not a spectrum of a named object. It is not a detection of a first-generation star. The Nature article is the only source attached here. There is no separate observatory release to lean on. The page is the journal article itself, and the account below stays inside what that public summary already supports.

## Heavy seeds, then a short feast

A seed, in this context, is the black hole left behind when a star collapses. It is the starting mass for everything that comes later. If the first stars are unusually massive, the black holes they leave are large from the start. You do not have to grow a stellar-mass remnant into a giant. You start partway there.

"Unusually" is doing a lot of quiet work. Getting first stars that heavy, inside a simulation, means choosing how their birth clouds behave. The choices that carry the result are less fine fragmentation, rapid accretion of the surrounding gas, and a different cooling history in metal-free clouds. Those are settings in the run. They are not new observations of a named first star delivered by this paper. Grant them, and the channel opens. Refuse them, and this particular route stays shut.

The second piece is a short episode of very fast growth. A seed buried in dense gas can pull material in furiously until the gas is cleared or the supply thins. In that window the black hole gains mass at a rate that looks outrageous next to a later galaxy where gas is scarce. The window ends. You do not need the black hole to eat at that rate for a billion years. You need the furious stretch early, while the surroundings are still thick. Front-loading is the whole trick. A polite rate, held for a long time, is the schedule that fails to finish. A heavy start plus a brief feast is the schedule the simulation uses instead.

## What "looks like a little red dot" means

Little red dots, as Webb finds them, are compact and red. They are easier to explain if a lot of the light is tied to a growing black hole than if it comes from a mature galaxy of ordinary stars. The simulation's objects come out similar: compact, red, and in that same interpretive neighborhood. Similarity is a comparison the authors are offering. It is not an identification of any particular dot in a Webb catalog. No dot is named. No redshift is claimed here. No mass is copied off a spectrum.

A mock population can resemble a real class without any mock object being the same as a catalogued dot. The useful statement is narrower. Given heavy seeds and dense early gas, a run can produce compact red sources and black holes already too heavy for a slow-growth story. The dots remain the clue. The run is one way to produce that clue without breaking the timeline.

## A channel, not a catch

A separate observed source, MoM-BH*-1, has been discussed as a black hole wrapped in a dense gas cocoon, and as a possible example of the kind of object a little red dot might be. That discussion is a spectrum and a fit to a real source. This Nature paper is a formation channel that could supply the black holes such dots might contain. The two results rhyme. They are not the same evidence. One starts from light collected from the sky. The other starts from a setup and grows a mock population.

If the channel works, the timing problem is less severe: the seeds were never small, and the growth spurt was loaded into the beginning. If the first stars were not that massive, the channel does not open, and the problem stands where Webb left it. Rapid growth falls out of a dense early environment only once the heavy seeds are granted. Granting them is the interpretive step.

The claim to keep is a possible route, not a discovery of heavy seeds in the sky. The run produced compact, red objects from seeds left by unusually massive first stars after a short interval of extremely fast growth. It did not detect a first star, name a dot, or prove that nature used this route. The Nature article is the authority for what the simulation included. The dots are still the clue in the data.

### Webb finds brown dwarfs only about twice Jupiter's mass

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-16_stars_tiny-brown-dwarfs/
- Published: 2026-09-16
- Topics: [Stars & Stellar Evolution](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/stars-and-stellar-evolution/)
- Freshness context: NASA and ESA released the IC 348 findings in September 2026, within the 15-day freshness window.
- Summary: In the star-forming region IC 348, about 1,000 light-years away in Perseus, Webb has found brown dwarfs with masses down to about twice Jupiter's, or 0.19 percent of the Sun's mass. They are the least massive brown dwarfs known, lighter than star-formation models predicted, and one of the lightest shows signs of a disk.
- Why it matters: The smallest stars weigh about 8 percent of the Sun. These objects formed by cloud collapse, like stars, yet sit near two Jupiter masses. That pushes the bottom of star formation below where the models had placed it, and it blurs any rule that tries to separate brown dwarfs from giant planets by mass alone.
- Suggested next question: How astronomers tell a brown dwarf born from a cloud from a giant planet born in a disk, when the masses overlap.
- Explore further: [NASA Science: Webb Reveals Dynamic Panorama of Star Formation](https://science.nasa.gov/missions/webb/nasas-webb-reveals-dynamic-panorama-of-star-formation/)
- Sources:
  - [NASA Science](https://science.nasa.gov/missions/webb/nasas-webb-reveals-dynamic-panorama-of-star-formation/)
  - [ESA Webb](https://esawebb.org/news/weic2619/)

Fuller note:

## Below the mass the models expected

IC 348 is a star-forming region about 1,000 light-years away, in the constellation Perseus. Cold clouds of molecular hydrogen collapse there and build new stars. The view Webb just released is one of the largest images the telescope has put out to the public. Astronomers used it to search for brown dwarfs, and they found objects down to about twice the mass of Jupiter.

A brown dwarf forms the way a star does, through the collapse of a molecular cloud, but its core never gets hot enough to fuse ordinary hydrogen into helium. Many brown dwarfs briefly fuse deuterium, a heavy form of hydrogen, early in their lives. The smallest true stars weigh about 8 percent of the Sun's mass. Below that line the object is a brown dwarf, even though the birth recipe was the same collapse that makes stars.

Twice Jupiter's mass is about 0.19 percent of the Sun's mass. NASA and ESA both call these the least massive brown dwarfs known, far smaller than theory predicted, and a challenge to models of how stars form. The data come from Webb General Observer Program 4866. ESA names the principal investigators as K. Luhman and C. Alves de Oliveira. NASA's image credit lists Kevin Luhman (PSU), Catarina Alves de Oliveira (ESA), and Mahdi Zamani (ESA/Webb). These releases identify program leadership and image credit, not a journal author list.

## From a wide image to a spectrum

The same team pointed Webb at IC 348 in 2022 and found brown dwarfs as light as three to four times Jupiter's mass. This pass goes lower. In 2024 they used NIRCam, Webb's Near-Infrared Camera, to catch the warm glow of young brown dwarfs and newborn stars in the new image. Candidates were selected from color and brightness. In 2025 they followed up with NIRSpec, the Near-Infrared Spectrograph, and used those spectra to study the masses.

Color and brightness only select a candidate. The mass comes from the later spectra. The releases state the floor and do not print an uncertainty beside it, so "twice Jupiter" is the precision they are willing to give.

The question taken to IC 348 was the bottom of star formation: how small an object can a collapsing cloud still make? The 2022 floor sat at a few Jupiter masses. The later spectra move the known floor to about two. That conflicts with the models the releases cite. It does not replace them. NASA and ESA state the challenge and do not say which piece of the theory has to move.

## A disk, a hydrocarbon, and maybe a class of their own

One of the lightest new brown dwarfs shows signs of a disk. NASA reads that as a hint that small planets could be forming around an object that itself has only about a planet's mass. ESA says planets could be forming around it even though the brown dwarf weighs about as much as a planet. The disk is the reported sign. Planets inside it are a suggestion, not a detection of a second object.

In the spectra, the team found a feature they attribute to a hydrocarbon, a molecule built only from hydrogen and carbon. NASA calls the carrier an unidentified hydrocarbon. The feature has been seen only in the atmospheres of the lowest-mass brown dwarfs, and the team suggests these objects might belong to a spectral class of their own. That is an inference from where the feature shows up, not a chemical identification with a lab match. A repeated bump can mean a shared atmosphere. It can also mean a shared temperature and haze.

Program 4866 has two further aims beyond the mass floor. One is to compare populations of planetary-mass objects between star-forming regions, and to see whether IC 348's tiny brown dwarfs are typical or local. The other is to chase the origin of the hydrocarbon feature in the lowest-mass objects. Both are questions the program is built to ask. Neither is answered by the image release alone.

## Jets in the same cloud, and a boundary drawn by mass

The upper right holds protostars still gathering mass. Several drive jets into nearby gas and dust, lighting Herbig-Haro objects, the glowing shocks those collisions make. HH 797, previously a Webb Picture of the Month, is two protostars with nearly parallel outflows. HH 211, just beside it, shows narrow jets and broader outflows in a propeller shape. A collage also marks the central cluster, fainter flows, gravitational lensing, and background spiral galaxies.

The cloud is still building ordinary stars, complete with outflows, while the census at the bottom has gone below the mass where the models were comfortable. Star formation here runs from massive stars that will explode in a few million years down to brown dwarfs of about two Jupiter masses.

Mass alone no longer sorts the recipes. A free-floating object of two Jupiter masses in a star-forming cloud can be a brown dwarf, born from collapse, with no star required. A planet grows inside a disk around a star. Jupiter shows that a disk can build something huge. These brown dwarfs show the other direction: cloud collapse did not stop where the models were comfortable. An isolated object with only a mass on the label inherits the ambiguity. Birthplace is what sorts them.

The releases do not say Jupiter formed by collapse, and they do not claim confirmed planets around these brown dwarfs. One of the lightest has signs of a disk. NASA's page and ESA's note weic2619 are the accounts to read before quoting the mass any more tightly than the agencies do.

### Feeding black holes may help build rings of new stars

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-15_black-holes_star-forming-rings/
- Published: 2026-09-15
- Topics: [Black Holes](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/black-holes/)
- Freshness context: Published in The Astrophysical Journal and announced by the Center for Astrophysics on 14 September 2026, within the 15-day freshness window.
- Summary: MUSE maps of nine nearby galaxies show the same layout around their feeding central black holes: rings or arcs of new stars, cones of black-hole radiation, and fast shocks in the gas. The pattern suggests these black holes sometimes help compress gas into stars, alongside the better-known habit of heating gas or driving it off.
- Why it matters: Black holes are usually cast as the reason star formation shuts down. A repeated pattern of young-star rings, radiation cones, and shocks in nine galaxies points to a mixed local effect. The same outflow that disturbs gas may also help some of it collapse. The maps show the layout. The compression is inferred.
- Suggested next question: How energy from a feeding black hole can either sweep gas away or squeeze some of it into new stars.
- Explore further: [Center for Astrophysics: New study reveals common pattern of black hole activity shaping nearby galaxies](https://www.cfa.harvard.edu/index.php/news/new-study-reveals-common-pattern-black-hole-activity-shaping-nearby-galaxies)
- Sources:
  - [Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian](https://www.cfa.harvard.edu/index.php/news/new-study-reveals-common-pattern-black-hole-activity-shaping-nearby-galaxies)
  - [The Astrophysical Journal](https://doi.org/10.3847/1538-4357/ae9956)
  - [scinexx](https://www.scinexx.de/news/kosmos/schwarze-loecher-koennten-sternbildung-mit-anstossen/)

Fuller note:

## The same pattern in nine galaxies

Nine nearby galaxies, each with a supermassive black hole still pulling gas in, show the same layout. Rings or arcs of new stars. Cone-shaped regions of energized gas. Fast shocks where outflows ram into that gas. The Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian announced the work from Cambridge on 14 September 2026, the day the paper came out in The Astrophysical Journal. The DOI is 10.3847/1538-4357/ae9956. A German-language account at scinexx is linked as another report of the study, not as a second dataset.

An active galactic nucleus, or AGN, is the bright center of a galaxy powered by gas falling onto a supermassive black hole. In the usual picture, energy coming back out heats gas or blows it away, and star formation shuts down. The new study says that picture is missing a direction. Actively growing black holes may also contribute to star formation in the host galaxy.

Nine is a modest sample, and large enough that the geometry is hard to file as one galaxy's quirk. The maps come from MUSE on the Very Large Telescope, which records optical light across a galaxy in space and in spectrum at once. Peixin Zhu, a graduate student at the Center for Astrophysics, says that once the galaxies were sharp enough, the black holes were seen pulling material in and throwing material out. The two motions are linked.

## Three colors for three power sources

The team used a three-dimensional diagnostic to separate, patch by patch, three ways to energize the gas. Star formation. Radiation from the active black hole. Excitation by shocks. A shock, in this paper's sense, happens when a high-speed outflow from the central black hole collides with the interstellar medium, the gas between the stars.

NGC 1386 is the galaxy they show as the worked example. In the zoomed map, red marks star formation, blue marks black-hole radiation, and yellow marks shocks. Across the full sample, star-forming rings or arcs appear about 0.8 to 6 kiloparsecs from the galactic center. A kiloparsec is their distance unit, thousands of light-years, so these rings sit well outside the nucleus and still inside the galaxy. Ionized cones of black-hole radiation extend outward from the disks. Regions dominated by fast shocks often run perpendicular to those bicones, the two-sided cones of radiation.

Zhu treats that right angle as the regular habit, not a one-off. The shocks go perpendicular to the direction of the black hole's injected outflows, and the arrangement shows up across all nine galaxies. The team reads the shocks as broadly consistent with jets from the AGN hitting the interstellar medium. Winds from the black hole may contribute as well, especially in galaxies whose jets are weaker. "Consistent with" is the right weight. The maps show where the shocks sit. The jet, or the wind, is the reading of why they sit there.

Lisa Kewley, an astrophysicist at the Center for Astrophysics, director of the center, and Zhu's advisor, describes black holes that do more than swallow material at the center. They reshape the surroundings. She frames the result as a look at a feedback cycle in galaxy evolution. Feedback, here, means energy leaving the black hole's vicinity and changing the gas that will or will not form the next stars.

## What was mapped, and what is inferred

Mapped with MUSE: the rings and arcs, the radiation cones, the shock zones, and the repeated right angle between shocks and outflows. Inferred: the same activity that stirs gas can also help compress some of it into new stars. Compression is a physical step between disturbed gas and a young star. The observations show the endpoints lined up in space. They do not follow one parcel of gas being squeezed and then lighting up. The inference is reasonable. It remains an inference.

Young stars have other reasons to form in rings. A bar, or a resonance in the disk, can pile gas up with no help from the black hole. The paper's case is that radiation and shocks sit with the rings in all nine systems, which would be a large coincidence if the nucleus were irrelevant. Closing that loophole is the job of the diagnostic and the models.

The study also compares the maps with theoretical models built by Zhu, Kewley, and Ralph Sutherland of the Australian National University, covering black-hole activity, star formation, and shocks. Chandra X-ray observations independently supported the reading. The announcement does not add a new X-ray number, so that support stays an independent check rather than a second map.

## A mixed local effect, not a new origin for galaxies

Gas falling into a black hole can release enough light and motion to empty gas from large regions. The same outflow can also hit a cloud along a shell or a ring and shove that cloud toward collapse. Both can be true in different places in the same galaxy. The nine-galaxy pattern is evidence that the second outcome shows up often enough to be a repeated structure.

Nothing here says black holes are net producers of stars, or that they assembled these galaxies. A net budget would need masses and rates the announcement does not give. The local claim is narrower: some gas is driven off, and some sits in a star-forming ring. The cycle the authors describe runs accretion, outflow, shock, and a change in where stars form.

The CfA release is the public account. The Astrophysical Journal paper is the authority for the measurements and the model comparison. scinexx is an additional report. Where the energy goes, and which gas it hits, decides whether the next stars are fewer or get a push.

### NASA and IBM released an open AI model trained on the Moon

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-14_solar-system_lunar-ai-model/
- Published: 2026-09-14
- Topics: [Solar System & Planetary Science](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/solar-system-and-planetary-science/)
- Freshness context: IBM announced the open-source NASA-IBM Lunar Foundation Model on 10 September 2026, within the 15-day freshness window.
- Summary: NASA and IBM have released an open-source AI model trained mostly on 17 years of Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter images, plus data from other Moon missions. Researchers can adapt it to map craters, spot odd volcanic patches, and estimate where polar ice might stay stable, using far less labeled data than a model built from scratch.
- Why it matters: The Moon is already mapped in enormous detail, and the data from one orbiter exceed the rest of NASA's planetary missions combined. A shared model that can read those maps together gives lunar scientists a faster way to date surfaces, revisit the Moon's volcanic past, and pick cold traps worth a closer look.
- Suggested next question: Why permanently shadowed craters near the Moon's poles can keep ice cold for up to billions of years.
- Explore further: [NASA: NASA, IBM Launch AI Foundation Model for Lunar Science](https://science.nasa.gov/science-research/artificial-intelligence-lunar-foundation-model/)
- Sources:
  - [NASA Science](https://science.nasa.gov/science-research/artificial-intelligence-lunar-foundation-model/)
  - [IBM Research](https://newsroom.ibm.com/2026-09-10-ibm-and-nasa-release-open-source-ai-model-to-support-lunar-exploration)

Fuller note:

## Trained on the Moon, released for other people to run

On 10 September 2026, IBM and NASA announced the NASA-IBM Lunar Foundation Model, an open-source AI system built for lunar science. IBM's newsroom carries that date. NASA's science page lists a last update of 9 September 2026. The weights are public on Hugging Face. The code is on GitHub. NASA describes it as among the first open-source AI models made specifically for the Moon, built with IBM Research and several academic groups.

A foundation model is a general model pre-trained on a huge unlabeled dataset, so a later job can adapt it with a smaller set of labeled examples instead of starting from scratch. Kevin Murphy, NASA's chief science data officer and acting chief data and AI officer, states the motive: the lunar record is already in hand, and petabytes of it still have to be easier to explore.

Most of the training material comes from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter. LRO has covered most of the lunar surface in detail for 17 years, and the mission's data volume is larger than all other NASA planetary missions combined. The model trained on roughly 2 million image tiles from that record: more than 1 million high-resolution camera images at 1-meter resolution, and nearly 964,000 multispectral images at 100-meter resolution. Other missions contributed high-resolution imagery and terrain too: NASA's GRAIL, NASA's Lunar Prospector, and JAXA's SELENE, also called Kaguya.

## Three jobs: craters, odd volcanoes, cold traps

Because the pre-training is already done, a planetary scientist can point the model at a specific question with only a small amount of labeled data. NASA names three jobs. Map craters. Spot young volcanic features. Estimate where ice may be stable near the poles, on the surface and below it.

Craters are the Moon's clock. Every crater is an impact, so counts and sizes date surfaces and, with them, stretches of solar system history. Doing that by hand is slow. The model is supposed to speed the finding and the measuring, and leave the interpretation to people who know what a crater count is for.

The volcanic job focuses on irregular mare patches, odd-looking volcanic features. The Moon is not thought to be active now, but these patches look young enough to push on the usual timelines for how fast the interior cooled. The model speeds the search. A person still has to decide whether a patch is a different kind of eruption or a trick of lighting.

Ice is the job with exploration attached. Permanently shadowed regions near the poles stay dark because crater rims block the Sun. NASA says those areas can remain cold enough to trap and preserve ice for up to billions of years. The model can help estimate where ice patches are likely to be stable, on the surface and below it. Stability is a calculation about cold, shadow, and depth: where ice, if it is there, would not boil off. A highlighted patch is a lead for the original maps, or for an instrument that can sense the hydrogen. It is not a core sample.

## Scores, and the dataset beside the model

NASA reports a performance check, and it is worth keeping separate from any new discovery. Across the tasks they evaluated, the lunar model matched or exceeded several strong baseline models. Crater mapping, and the segmentation of irregular mare patches, came out comparable to those baselines. Polar ice stability is where NASA says the model showed a clear advantage. That is a score on a benchmark. It is not a newly confirmed ice deposit with a latitude and a depth.

IBM describes the companion data: what they call the first open lunar dataset of its kind for machine learning, with more than 30 spatially aligned layers, nine instruments, four missions, and tens of thousands of images and maps. LRO and GRAIL supply much of it, with SELENE/Kaguya adding surface and subsurface layers. NASA also released pre-training sets and benchmarks, and folded the model into the open TerraTorch toolkit. A companion paper on Hugging Face is titled "Multimodal-Multiresolution Foundation Model for Lunar Remote Sensing."

Juan Bernabe-Moreno, director of IBM Research Europe in the UK and Ireland, describes the point of the release as a base scientists can adapt, so observations from different instruments can be read together. The model joins the Prithvi family, earlier open foundation models from the same collaboration, covering geospatial data, weather, and heliophysics. The Moon is the new domain.

Inside NASA, the Impact AI team at Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville built the model with the Planetary Science Division, Goddard, and Ames. The science team includes the Universities Space Research Association, the SETI Institute, the University of Maryland, Baltimore County, Howard University, and NASA researchers at headquarters, Ames, and Goddard.

## A tool, not a new patch of ground truth

Both public accounts describe a tool and a dataset. They do not describe a patch of ground the model discovered and lunar scientists have already confirmed. The inventory is a pre-trained model, a stack of aligned maps, three tasks, and a benchmark where ice-stability estimates are the clearest gain.

A model trained to generalize can smooth over a rare feature, or draw an edge the pixels did not have. Crater counts and ice maps later get quoted in mission plans, so anything from this model needs a check against the original images. Murphy's hope of new discoveries is a statement at launch. The discoveries would be later papers.

Use NASA's page for the tasks, the tile counts, and the scores. Use IBM's note for the open dataset and the Prithvi context. Use a later study for any named crater or any claim that ice sits in a particular cold trap.

### Around half of neutron stars may form as magnetars

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-13_stars-magnetars-neutron-stars/
- Published: 2026-09-13
- Topics: [Stars & Stellar Evolution](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/stars-and-stellar-evolution/)
- Freshness context: Published in Nature Astronomy on 10 September 2026, within the 15-day freshness window.
- Summary: A Nature Astronomy study finds that magnetars, neutron stars with extremely strong magnetic fields, could make up around half the neutron star population. The figure comes from a simulation of how these remnants evolve, not from a fresh headcount.
