If it holds, magnetars are common enough to help power some of the brightest explosions and radio flashes astronomers see.
- Why it matters: Superluminous supernovae, gamma-ray bursts, and fast radio bursts need a strong central engine often enough that a rare magnetar birth rate has been hard to square with the flashes on record. A birth fraction near half would make that supply much easier to imagine in the Milky Way. Other galaxies remain the test.
- Suggested next question: How a neutron star's magnetic field can decay until an object born as a magnetar later looks like a pulsar or a quiet X-ray source.
- Explore further: [Nature Astronomy: The magnetar fraction in core-collapse supernovae](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-026-02915-5)
- Sources:
  - [Nature Astronomy](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-026-02915-5)
  - [Institute of Space Studies of Catalonia (IEEC)](https://www.ieec.cat/en/half-of-the-neutron-stars-could-be-magnetars/)

Fuller note:

## Half, from a model of whole lives

A magnetar is a neutron star with an extremely strong magnetic field. A paper in Nature Astronomy on 10 September 2026 says magnetars could make up around 50 percent of the neutron star population, on average. The study was led by researchers at the Institute of Space Studies of Catalonia, working at the Institute of Space Sciences (ICE-CSIC) in Barcelona. Celsa Pardo Araujo, a predoctoral researcher, is first author. Nanda Rea, M. Ronchi, and V. Graber are the other authors. The paper's title is "Magnetar fraction in Core-Collapse Supernovae."

The method is population synthesis. A computer follows neutron stars from the supernova that makes them to the objects in today's catalogs. Nobody walked the Milky Way and tagged half the neutron stars by hand. The 50 percent is the fraction the simulation prefers once it has to match the stars we already see, including objects that look different as they age.

The galaxy they live in is crowded. The Milky Way holds about one hundred billion stars. About one percent of them, roughly one hundred million, are neutron stars, collapsed cores left when massive stars explode. Magnetars have been filed as the rare tail of that crowd. That rarity is awkward if they are supposed to power superluminous supernovae, gamma-ray bursts, and fast radio bursts, events that need a strong central engine often enough that a small birth supply struggles to keep up.

## Four labels, one life story

A neutron star does not keep one job title. Radio pulsars sweep beams of radio waves past Earth, so we see pulses. Magnetars carry the extreme fields and are prone to bursts. Central compact objects are the young neutron stars found in the middle of supernova remnants, often quiet at radio wavelengths. X-ray isolated neutron stars glow from their leftover heat and lack the usual pulses. Recent studies had already pointed to evolutionary links among these classes. A strong field can decay. A fast spin can slow. An object born looking like a magnetar can spend a later chapter looking like one of the others.

Earlier counts, the IEEC account says, assumed magnetars were relatively rare and left those links out. Count only the objects that still look like magnetars today and you will miss the ones that were magnetars and have since faded into another class. The birth fraction and the present-day headcount are not the same number. Pardo Araujo's point is that the types have to be modeled together, connections included, before the fraction that forms is a fair estimate.

This is the first population synthesis, the team says, that puts the main types of isolated neutron stars into one framework at the same time. Isolated means no companion star is feeding them or spinning them up. The model takes in galactic dynamics, meaning where the stars sit and how they move. It takes in spin-down, the slowing of the rotation. It takes in magneto-thermal evolution, the joint change of temperature and magnetic field across a life. Observational bias goes in too, so the fit has to respect which objects the surveys can actually catch. From that single fit the authors infer two things at once: the magnetar fraction, and how many supernova explosions the Milky Way needs.

## A supernova rate, then a fraction

The explosions in question are core-collapse supernovae. They come from stars of about 8 to 25 times the Sun's mass. The star exhausts the fuel that makes it shine, gravity wins, and the core collapses into a neutron star. Reproducing the neutron stars astronomers actually detect requires a core-collapse rate above two per century in the observed population. In calendar terms: more than two such explosions in the Milky Way every hundred years. Without that rate, the model cannot stock the galaxy with the remnants already on the books.

The team got the rate two ways that do not share the same pile of data. First, from supernova remnants still visible. Second, from the number of neutron stars detected in the galaxy. Knowing the rate is what lets them turn a census of survivors into a statement about births. Given that rate, the study suggests magnetars would represent, on average, around 50 percent of the neutron star population. Much more common, they say, than previous studies had indicated.

The 50 percent is an average from a fit. Pardo Araujo concludes that if magnetars really are this common, they could account for a significant share of the most energetic flashes, including fast radio bursts, gamma-ray bursts, and superluminous supernovae. The flashes were not newly pinned to named magnetars. The birth supply is no longer obviously too small.

## The check that needs other galaxies

What went in was the Milky Way's remnants, counts, spins, temperatures, and positions, plus the known holes in the surveys. What came out was a fraction and a supernova rate. The published figure is an average from that fit, not a direct headcount.

Nanda Rea calls the next step a natural extension: try the same synthesis outside the Milky Way. Predict a galaxy's magnetar population, then set it next to the observed rates of superluminous supernovae, fast radio bursts, and gamma-ray bursts. The comparison needs that galaxy's star-formation history, because the core-collapse rate may not match ours.

Until those comparisons exist, the 50 percent stays a Milky Way result. Nature Astronomy carries the model. The IEEC note is the public walk-through. Neither is a stack of new magnetars. The open question is whether many pulsars and X-ray sources are the same kind of birth, seen at different ages.

### A proto-supercluster caught while the universe was 2.1 billion years old

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-12_cosmology_proto-supercluster-cosmos-z3-1-a/
- Published: 2026-09-12
- Topics: [Cosmology & Early Universe](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/cosmology-and-early-universe/)
- Freshness context: Published in The Astrophysical Journal on 8 September 2026.
- Summary: COSMOS-z3.1-A is a proto-supercluster, a clumpy gathering of galaxies that has not finished merging, seen when the universe was 2.1 billion years old. ODIN imaging and follow-up spectra from DESI, Gemini South, and Keck place it earlier than the proto-supercluster Hyperion. Its mass is 5000 times that of the Milky Way, and the team expects fewer than one such object per 10,000 galaxy clusters.
- Why it matters: Nearby superclusters are finished products. COSMOS-z3.1-A still shows separate clumps sitting where several filaments of the cosmic web cross. That layout lets astronomers test the bottom-up picture, in which small structures form first and later merge, against a real object from when the universe was young.
- Suggested next question: Follow how galaxy groups and protoclusters merge along the cosmic web into the clusters we see nearby.
- Explore further: [NSF NOIRLab: Extremely massive galaxy proto-supercluster smashes distance records](https://noirlab.edu/public/news/noirlab2622/)
- Sources:
  - [NSF NOIRLab](https://noirlab.edu/public/news/noirlab2622/)
  - [Rutgers University](https://newbrunswick.rutgers.edu/news/scientists-see-one-universes-largest-structures-taking-shape)
  - [The Astrophysical Journal](https://doi.org/10.3847/1538-4357/ae8091)

Fuller note:

## A supercluster that has not collapsed yet

Galaxy clusters are the most massive gravitationally bound structures in the universe: hundreds to thousands of galaxies, spanning millions of light-years, held together mostly by dark matter. Nearby clusters are mature. They grew out of protoclusters, enormous loosely bound collections of galaxies that are still merging and have not settled.

A proto-supercluster is one step larger and one step less finished. It is the ancestor of a cluster of clusters, several over-dense pieces that belong to one structure and have not yet fallen into a single relaxed system. COSMOS-z3.1-A is that kind of object. NSF NOIRLab's announcement calls it the earliest, most distant proto-supercluster yet identified. The paper, "ODIN: Characterizing the Three-dimensional Structure of Two Protocluster Complexes at z = 3.1," is in The Astrophysical Journal, 8 September 2026, DOI 10.3847/1538-4357/ae8091.

COSMOS is the sky field. The label z3.1 is a redshift: expansion has stretched the light, and that stretch marks how long the light has been traveling. The team places this structure at a time when the universe was only 2.1 billion years old. Another proto-supercluster, Hyperion, had already been reported. COSMOS-z3.1-A is identified at an even earlier time.

## From a wide camera to a depth map

The search leans on the ODIN survey, One-hundred-deg2 DECam Imaging in Narrowbands. DECam, the Dark Energy Camera, was fabricated for the Department of Energy. It has a 570-megapixel detector and sits on the U.S. National Science Foundation's Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory in Chile, a program of NSF NOIRLab. With that wide field, DECam spent more than 100 nights over the last three years taking deep images across a huge area of the southern sky.

An international team led by Vandana Ramakrishnan, a graduate student at Purdue University at the time of the study, used those images to look for young cluster progenitors. In total they identified 150 distant protoclusters, formed when the universe was about 1 to 3 billion years old. They then focused on two striking overdensities, COSMOS-z3.1-A and COSMOS-z3.1-C. The COSMOS field is a useful place for this work. It looks away from the crowded plane of the Milky Way, and many of the major telescopes have already spent time there.

ODIN supplied the flat coordinates, positions on the sky. A structure this large needs a third dimension, or a chance alignment of unrelated galaxies can mimic a pile-up. Spectrographs turn a spectrum into a distance. Ramakrishnan was joined by Byeongha Moon of the Korea Astronomy and Space Science Institute and Nicole Firestone of Rutgers University to lead that follow-up. Rutgers's news post is the other institutional account of a structure still taking shape.

Most of the spectra come from DESI, the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument, which can measure distances to 5000 galaxies at once. DESI was built with Department of Energy support and international partners, is operated with DOE funding, and is managed by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. It rides on the NSF Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory in Arizona. Additional spectra come from the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph on Gemini South in Chile, and from the Deep Imaging Multi-Object Spectrograph, DEIMOS, on the Keck II telescope on Maunakea in Hawaii.

## Heavier than Coma, rarer than a typical cluster

The 3D maps let the team predict what these structures grow into. Both COSMOS-z3.1-A and COSMOS-z3.1-C are expected to become more massive than the Coma Cluster, the largest known galaxy cluster in the local universe. A is the rarer object. It is a proto-supercluster, with a mass 5000 times that of the Milky Way. Ramakrishnan describes it as one of the most extreme, most overdense regions, and the team thinks there should be fewer than one such object for every 10,000 galaxy clusters.

Those are strong claims, and they should stay attached to the map. The observation is many galaxies, confirmed as members, concentrated in clumps at this redshift, tied together in three dimensions. The forecast, more massive than Coma, is a prediction of future growth, not a weighing of a finished cluster. The rarity, fewer than one per 10,000 clusters, is the team's estimate of how unusual the overdensity is. A record also depends on definitions. Hyperion shows that the category already had a member. This object's claim is that it sits earlier.

A visualization with the NOIRLab note marks confirmed members of COSMOS-z3.1-A as light-blue circles. Purple marks the thicker knots of galaxy density. A. Ortiz at Purdue built the original 3D model.

## Clumps where several filaments cross

The maps show the protoclusters as very clumpy and irregular. They lie at the intersections of multiple filaments of the cosmic web, the large-scale network of matter. NOIRLab reports this as the first time such features have been directly observed in the distant universe. The layout agrees with expectations for how matter is distributed.

Current models build structure from the bottom up. Smaller pieces form first and merge into larger ones. The clumps in these maps read as that unfinished merging. Over time the clumps should collapse together and leave clusters closer in shape to the rounder systems seen nearby. Ramakrishnan's aim for the project matches that test: the growth of massive structures, the effect those structures have on the galaxies inside them, and the way protoclusters connect to the web.

The 3D method separates a core, an outskirts, and a filament still feeding the system. In the coming decade the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time will image the southern sky every few nights, and the overlap with ODIN can follow cluster growth across cosmic time. That survey is a plan. The measurement in hand is the pair of complexes at redshift 3.1, caught while the pieces were still separate.

### Tiny worlds beyond Neptune still carry the colors of their birth

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-11_solar-system_tiny-worlds-beyond-neptune/
- Published: 2026-09-11
- Topics: [Solar System & Planetary Science](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/solar-system-and-planetary-science/)
- Freshness context: Published in The Astronomical Journal and announced by NASA on 8 September 2026.
- Summary: Hubble and Webb together found 27 previously unknown worlds beyond Neptune, some only about 5 kilometres across, in the deepest survey of these bodies so far. Their surface colors match the relations seen in much larger objects, in both the cold and the hot dynamical families. The size distributions of the two families look similar, and very small bodies are fewer than some formation models expected.
- Why it matters: Beyond Neptune, dust and pebbles built city-sized planetesimals and then stopped, so these icy bodies are leftovers from planet building, including the material that went into worlds like Earth. Their colors still carry a birthplace signature. That record is cleaner than a collision-reworked surface would have been, and it is still incomplete: hot-family orbits were scrambled long ago.
- Suggested next question: Explore the Kuiper Belt, the icy region beyond Neptune, and ask which surface clues survive after giant planets rearrange orbits.
- Explore further: [NASA: Hubble and Webb find far-out Solar System objects that remember their past](https://science.nasa.gov/missions/hubble/nasas-hubble-webb-find-far-out-solar-system-objects-remember-past/)
- Sources:
  - [NASA Science](https://science.nasa.gov/missions/hubble/nasas-hubble-webb-find-far-out-solar-system-objects-remember-past/)
  - [NASA Scientific Visualization Studio](https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/15092)

Fuller note:

## Twenty-seven faint points, smaller than the ground can reach

For the first time, teams used NASA's Hubble and James Webb space telescopes together on some of the most distant small bodies in the Solar System. These are trans-Neptunian objects, TNOs: icy worlds orbiting the Sun beyond Neptune. Even with both telescopes they remain points of light. An artist's concept in the NASA release is explicit about that. The bodies are too small to show a disk.

Two papers in The Astronomical Journal, published with NASA's announcement on 8 September 2026, cover the sample. One paper takes color and composition. The other takes the size distribution. The sample is 27 newly discovered tiny, dim TNOs, found in the deepest survey of these objects so far. NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio posted a short film the same day, a visual companion to the science release. The papers are the authority for the photometry and the sizes.

Most TNOs are more than 100 million times dimmer than a star you can see by eye. The smallest diameter in this set is about 3 miles, or 5 kilometres, about five times smaller than the most sensitive ground-based surveys can pick out. One object is so faint that NASA compares it to standing on Earth and seeing a small swarm of fireflies on the Moon. Webb is what reached those sizes. Hubble supplied the visible light. Webb supplied the infrared. Together they measure colors, sizes, and orbits that either telescope would have left incomplete.

## Planetesimals that never finished the second step

This population is a leftover from an early stage of planet building. A disk of dust and pebbles around the young Sun clumped into city-sized planetesimals, the solid building blocks that later merge into planets. Beyond Neptune that second stage did not happen. The planetesimals stayed a frozen population. The Kuiper Belt, a doughnut-shaped region of icy objects beyond Neptune and home to Pluto, is the neighbourhood these surveys are sampling. This particular search is one deep patch, not a full census of the belt.

The teams were led by PhD candidates at the University of Victoria, with guidance from the National Research Council of Canada, and at Northern Arizona University in Flagstaff. Anastasia Morgan at Northern Arizona led the study of color and composition. Marielle Eduardo at Victoria led the study of sizes. David Trilling of Northern Arizona is a coauthor.

Color, in this work, is a rough fingerprint of the surface: ices and the reddening material mixed through them. Orbits sort the objects into dynamical families. Dynamically cold TNOs travel on relatively circular paths in the plane of the Solar System, thought to be near where they formed. Dynamically hot TNOs formed between the current locations of Uranus and Neptune. When the outer giant planets migrated, early in Solar System history, those bodies were pushed outward. Today they ride highly elliptical orbits and move in and out of the plane.

## The small ones still wear the family colors

Before these observations, astronomers expected many collisions. Small TNOs in both families should have had their surfaces refreshed or altered, so the tiniest bodies ought to show different colors from Pluto-scale objects. The data go the other way. The small bodies look like their larger counterparts. Both the hot and the cold populations seem to keep the colors they had when they formed, with little change since the birth of the Solar System.

Morgan's image for that result is memory. Knocking a body around and breaking it up could have changed the surface composition, and then tiny TNOs would wear a different color from their larger siblings. The smallest objects are instead preserving the history of how they were made. Trilling's point is about place. The hot TNOs still carry a signature of where they were born, even after their orbits were scrambled.

The color match has two readings, and the teams have not separated them. Collisions may be rarer than expected, so surfaces were never much reworked. Or collisions happen, and the bodies somehow keep their original, pre-collision composition anyway. Either reading leaves the ices as a cleaner record than a heavily reprocessed population would have offered. Cleaner is not complete. The hot family's orbits were rearranged. The surface chemistry is what seems to have held.

## Same sizes in two birthplaces, and fewer pebbles at the end

Webb also let the researchers count how many objects appear at each size. The overall size distributions of the hot and cold populations are similar, even though the two families formed in different parts of the early disk. Eduardo's suggestion is that planetesimal formation does not care much about those local conditions. The process produced similar sizes whether the disk was hot or cold, and whether it was dense or fluffy. That is a suggestion about a process, drawn from one deep field.

The other size result is a shortage. There are fewer of these very small bodies than some planet-formation models predicted. The shortage is relative to those models. It is not a claim that the region beyond Neptune is empty. Ground surveys simply could not see a 5-kilometre body at these distances. A joint Hubble and Webb campaign could, barely, and the faint end came out thinner than the models had sketched.

Hold the measurements apart from the stories. The measurements are 27 new TNOs, colors that follow the large-object relations in both families, similar size distributions, and fewer very small bodies than some models expected. The stories are fewer collisions, or tough primordial surfaces, and a formation process that is insensitive to disk conditions. The Astronomical Journal papers are where those stories have to survive the photometry.

### Chandra's archive hid 84 ultralow-energy sources in six galaxies

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-10_stars-stellar-evolution_chandra-hypersoft-sources/
- Published: 2026-09-10
- Topics: [Stars & Stellar Evolution](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/stars-and-stellar-evolution/)
- Freshness context: Published in Nature Astronomy on 9 September 2026.
- Summary: A search of the public Chandra archive found 84 hypersoft X-ray sources in six galaxies, including the spirals M31 and M101. They show up at the lowest X-ray energies and disappear at higher ones, with most of their power in ultraviolet light that gas between the stars absorbs. The leading idea is a white dwarf, neutron star, or black hole pulling gas from a companion. The class is new. The identity is not settled.
- Why it matters: Some white-dwarf versions of these binaries may be the systems that later explode as Type Ia supernovae, the blasts used to measure cosmic expansion. Their ultraviolet output may also help strip electrons from gas between stars, a job hot massive stars do not finish alone. Both ideas stay conditional until the compact object in each source is identified.
- Suggested next question: Follow how a white dwarf can gain mass from a companion and how astronomers use the resulting Type Ia supernova to measure cosmic expansion.
- Explore further: [Nature Astronomy: Hypersoft X-ray sources as a low-energy class of luminous cosmic emitter](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-026-02959-7)
- Sources:
  - [Nature Astronomy](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-026-02959-7)
  - [NASA Chandra X-ray Observatory](https://science.nasa.gov/missions/chandra/nasas-chandra-unveils-mysterious-x-ray-objects/)

Fuller note:

## Sources that appear, then vanish, as the energy rises

Using NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory, a team found a class of objects that does not behave like the X-ray sources astronomers already file. Mustafa Muhibullah of the University of Alabama led the study. The paper in Nature Astronomy, published on 9 September 2026, names them hypersoft X-ray sources. Soft X-rays are the lower-energy ones. Hypersoft means softer still: the emission piles up at the bottom of the X-ray band, so low that most of the power sits in energetic ultraviolet light next door on the spectrum.

The search used data already public in the Chandra archive. The team found 84 of these sources in six galaxies. Two of the galaxies are spirals, M31, the Andromeda galaxy, and M101, the Pinwheel galaxy. The other four are ellipticals. The sources turn up both in regions of active star formation and in places dominated by older stars. They are not confined to one kind of stellar neighbourhood.

The selection trick is almost blunt. Find objects present in Chandra images taken at the lowest X-ray energies, then check the higher-energy images. These sources vanish there. Far more low-energy X-rays than high-energy ones. Because low-energy X-rays border ultraviolet radiation, the team infers a large ultraviolet output as well. In the release's composite image of M101, most specks are ordinary stellar pairs. Seven of the specks are members of this new class, marked so a reader can see how ordinary they look.

## A binary is the leading idea, not a finished ID

What produces that spectrum is not settled. The team thinks the sources most likely involve a black hole, a neutron star, or a white dwarf pulling material from a companion star. Gas drawn off the companion heats up and radiates before it falls onto the white dwarf or the neutron star, or into the black hole. Binaries like that have been seen before. They have not been seen with this combination of bright ultraviolet radiation and such low-energy X-rays.

Muhibullah's summary is that the group does not act like objects the field had already encountered, and that these easily missed sources are actually among the most energetic objects in galaxies. "Most energetic" can coexist with "hypersoft." Energy is the total power. Soft describes where on the spectrum that power comes out. A lamp can be bright and still shine in a band your camera barely records.

The discovery suggests large populations of ultraviolet-bright binaries may have gone undetected. That is a population claim, still a suggestion. It follows from finding 84 sources once the archive was searched in the right energy slice, and from the reasons, below, that the slice is hard to search.

## Two problems they might help with

Both payoffs are conditional. Treat them as jobs these objects might be doing, not as jobs already assigned.

Some white-dwarf systems that pull mass from a companion may later explode as Type Ia supernovae. Those explosions are a standard tool for measuring how fast the universe is expanding. They also played a key role in the discovery that the expansion is accelerating. Astronomers have looked for the stars that become Type Ia supernovae for many years, so far without a clear success. Coauthor Jimmy Irwin, also at the University of Alabama, puts the gap in time order. The explosions are studied after they happen. What actually ignites is still hard to pin down. Spotting the systems beforehand would change that. "Could be on the way to a supernova" is not a count of how many of the 84 will explode, or when. Only the white-dwarf branch of the candidate list even has that future. Neutron stars and black holes do not explode as Type Ia events.

The other problem is closer to home inside a galaxy. Something strips electrons off gas between the stars. That ionization affects how quickly stars form and how a galaxy's gas evolves. Hot, massive stars do part of the work. They do not fully explain it. The intense ultraviolet radiation from hypersoft sources may supply some of the missing photons. Again, a plausible role, not a measured fraction of the ionizing budget.

## Why the archive could hide something this bright

Two barriers kept the class out of earlier catalogues. Low-energy X-rays are difficult for X-ray telescopes to detect. And the high-energy ultraviolet light is readily absorbed by hydrogen and helium gas between the stars, a nearly opaque screen along the line of sight. You do not get a clean ultraviolet picture. You get a soft X-ray tail that is easy to miss if the pipeline is tuned for harder sources. That is a selection effect. A bright population can sit in a public archive and still be skipped.

Rosanne Di Stefano of the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard and Smithsonian, a coauthor, describes the archive search as the way past that blind spot. Chandra can catch the soft X-ray tail. It cannot, from these data alone, weigh the compact object or watch the companion star.

NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, manages the Chandra program. The Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory's Chandra X-ray Center runs science operations from Cambridge, Massachusetts, and flight operations from Burlington, Massachusetts. Those are the institutions behind the telescope. The scientific authority for the sample and the spectra is the Nature Astronomy article. Until a follow-up weighs the compact object, the remnant list stays open: white dwarf, neutron star, or black hole, each with a companion, each still allowed.

### Fast radio bursts trace ordinary matter the galaxies have pushed around

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-09_cosmology_fast-radio-bursts-hidden-matter/
- Published: 2026-09-09
- Topics: [Cosmology & Early Universe](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/cosmology-and-early-universe/)
- Freshness context: Published in Nature Astronomy on 8 September 2026.
- Summary: About 100 fast radio bursts, millisecond radio flashes from distant galaxies, carry a delay that counts electrons along the path. A Nature Astronomy analysis uses that delay to measure how galactic feedback smooths ordinary matter around and between galaxies. The smoothing is real, and it is weaker than earlier results from eROSITA and the Atacama Cosmology Telescope. Dark matter is not what the bursts see.
- Why it matters: Surveys of cosmic clumping are used to study dark energy, dark matter, and the neutrino mass. Feedback from black holes and exploding stars smooths gas in a way that can imitate those signals. An independent fast-radio-burst measurement of that smoothing gives the surveys a feedback term they can subtract, from a sample of only about 100 bursts.
- Suggested next question: Trace the cosmic web of galaxies, gas, and dark matter, and ask which parts a radio delay can count.
- Explore further: [Nature Astronomy: Signatures of suppressed matter clustering revealed by fast radio bursts](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-026-02957-9)
- Sources:
  - [Nature Astronomy](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-026-02957-9)
  - [Caltech](https://www.caltech.edu/about/news/fast-radio-bursts-poised-to-help-with-biggest-cosmic-mysteries)

Fuller note:

## A millisecond flash, then a frequency delay

Fast radio bursts are intense, brief flashes of radio light. They last about a millisecond and can cross billions of light-years before they reach Earth. On the way they pass through a thin fog of ordinary matter. Ordinary matter here means baryons: protons, neutrons, the particles that build gas, stars, planets, and people. A large share of those baryons is not locked in galaxies. It is spread through the space around and between them, ionized and faint.

The fog changes the radio signal. Lower frequencies arrive later than higher ones. Astronomers call the size of that delay a dispersion measure: a count of the electrons along the path. More electrons, more delay. Caltech's account compares the spreading to a prism sorting white light into colours. The concrete observable is simpler than the analogy. You time the sweep from high frequency to low, subtract the electrons in the Milky Way, and what remains is a backlight on the gas between here and the burst.

The bursts' own engines are a separate uncertainty. Magnetars, neutron stars with extreme magnetic fields, are a possible source. That idea is not a settled identification for every burst. You do not need the engine to use the delay. You need the distance, the frequency sweep, and a model of what else sits on the path. Those subtractions are where the measurement can go wrong, which is why the paper, not this note, is the authority.

## Feedback can wear a cosmological costume

A Nature Astronomy paper published on 8 September 2026 uses a sample of about 100 bursts. The title is "Signatures of suppressed matter clustering revealed by fast radio bursts." Kritti Sharma, a graduate student at Caltech working with Vikram Ravi, a professor of astronomy there, led the study. Elisabeth Krause, a professor of astronomy and physics at the University of Arizona, is a coauthor. Also on the paper: Pranjal R. S. at Arizona, Dhayaa Anbajagane at the University of Chicago, and Liam Connor at the Harvard and Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics.

Dark energy, dark matter, and neutrinos all enter the story as reasons to care, not as things this sample claims to have weighed. Dark energy is the name for whatever is driving the universe to expand faster and faster. Dark matter far outweighs ordinary matter and does not shine. Neutrinos pass through ordinary matter almost undisturbed, and their mass would change how large structures grew. All three are predicted to influence how matter clumps. Sky surveys map that clumping to get at them.

Galaxies muddy the map. Supermassive black holes in galaxy centres blow winds of hot, ionized gas. Exploding stars dump energy into the neighbourhood. Astronomers call this feedback. It moves gas outward and makes the matter distribution smoother. Ravi's point is the costume: the smoothing can look a great deal like the signature of massive neutrinos, or like some versions of dark energy and dark matter. Unless someone measures the feedback piece on its own, those effects cannot be told apart.

## What a hundred bursts actually delivered

This sample is the first to measure the impact of feedback on clumpy matter directly, in the large-scale regions around and between galaxies. The result: feedback does smooth the gas. It does so less than earlier measurements from the eROSITA X-ray telescope and from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope, a microwave survey in Chile that ended in 2022. "Less" is the result. The paper does not hand this notebook a second number for how much less. The comparison is the claim to keep.

Krause's assessment is that the constraint is already competitive with those X-ray and microwave surveys, from only about 100 bursts. She calls that a beginning. Sharma's line is that these data can be used to sharpen cosmology experiments aimed at dark matter, dark energy, and the neutrino mass. That is a use. It is not a completed answer to any of the three.

Dispersion traces electrons, which trace ionized ordinary matter. It does not see dark matter. Its power is negative in a useful way. It stops dark-matter and dark-energy analyses from quietly absorbing a baryon effect they did not measure. Separate the sentences. The measurement is a degree of smoothing, weaker than the X-ray and microwave ones. The interpretation is that galactic feedback produced that smoothing. The hope, still ahead of the data, is a cleaner subtraction inside other surveys.

## Catalogues that do not exist yet

The sample is small next to what is being built. Caltech's Deep Synoptic Array, scheduled for a remote valley in Nevada by 2029 and funded by Schmidt Sciences, is expected to find tens of thousands of bursts. Ravi, a co-principal investigator, expects that catalogue to work alongside the European Euclid mission, DESI in Arizona, the Vera Rubin Observatory in Chile, and NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory and Caltech's IPAC centre have roles in Euclid and Roman. Caltech manages JPL for NASA. Those are plans and partnerships. The Nature Astronomy result is the hundred-burst measurement.

One practical distinction survives the plans. A fast radio burst is a backlight on electrons. Electrons flag ordinary matter the galaxies have pushed around. They do not weigh the dark sector. They make it harder to mistake that pushed-around gas for a new particle or a new property of expansion.

### Two massive stars still forming look captured, not born as a pair

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-08_stars-stellar-evolution_massive-binary-capture/
- Published: 2026-09-08
- Topics: [Stars & Stellar Evolution](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/stars-and-stellar-evolution/)
- Freshness context: Published in Nature Astronomy on 7 September 2026.
- Summary: ALMA, the VLA, JWST, and the VLT mapped IRAS 07299-1651, two massive protostars still growing inside a molecular cloud. Nearly eight years of positions show an elongated orbit, and the disks around the two stars tilt relative to each other and to that orbit. A shared birth in one disk has trouble with that geometry. A later close encounter fits it better.
- Why it matters: Many massive stars live with a companion, and the companion changes how they exchange mass, spin, and die. This system is one case where the orbit and the tilted disks favor capture after separate births. A single shared disk would have lined the stars and the disks up together. One system shows a route. It does not yet show how common that route is.
- Suggested next question: Ask why so many massive stars have companions, and how a partner changes the path from birth to explosion.
- Explore further: [Nature Astronomy: An eccentric massive protobinary assembled via a core-merger parabolic encounter](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-026-02953-z)
- Sources:
  - [Nature Astronomy](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-026-02953-z)
  - [ALMA Observatory](https://alma-telescope.jp/news/mbassemble-202609.html)

Fuller note:

## A pair still growing, on a stretched path

Many stars in the Milky Way are born with a companion. Among massive stars the pairing is especially common. A companion changes what happens next: mass can move from one star to the other, spins can be driven up, and the deaths of massive stars often look different when a partner is present. How the partnership starts is less settled. The stars might have collapsed out of one shared core, already bound. Or they might have formed apart and been captured later.

IRAS 07299-1651 is a concrete case. It holds two massive protostars, still growing by pulling in gas, buried in a molecular cloud. An international team led by Yichen Zhang of Shanghai Jiao Tong University used the ALMA telescope to watch them. The Nature Astronomy paper, published on 7 September 2026, is led by Yao Wang, a doctoral student at the same university. The title states the preferred history in technical language: an eccentric massive protobinary assembled via a core-merger parabolic encounter.

Eccentric means the orbit is elongated, far from a tidy circle. A parabolic encounter is a close pass on a path that is just barely unbound, the kind of flyby that can end in capture if the pair loses a little energy during the meeting. Core-merger, in this usage, points at two dense star-forming cores that meet and become one bound system. The ALMA Observatory's Japanese release is the other account attached to this note.

## Eight years of tiny shifts on the sky

An earlier ALMA look at the same object had already found the embedded pair and studied its motions. Those results lined up, roughly, with a familiar picture: a large gas disk splits and the two stars form together. One detail sat badly in that picture. The disks around the two protostars looked misaligned.

To test the orbit, the team measured tiny proper motions, the slow drift of each star's position on the sky. That measurement needs ALMA's angular resolution and its ability to pin positions. Stitching together observations that span nearly eight years, they caught slight shifts that trace orbital motion. Zhang's description of the result is direct. For the first time, they were seeing two massive stars, still being born, orbiting each other.

ALMA did not work alone. The three-dimensional picture combines ALMA data at several wavelengths with the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array, the James Webb Space Telescope, and the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope. Kei Tanaka, an assistant professor at the Institute of Science Tokyo and a coauthor, notes that the multi-wavelength ALMA data also narrowed the protostellar masses the orbit fit needs. Webb and the other infrared views located the jets, the narrow streams blowing away from the stars. ALMA resolved the compact disk around each protostar. Hydrogen recombination lines, shifted red or blue by the Doppler effect, show which way those ionized disks are spinning. Gas coming toward us shifts one way. Gas going away shifts the other. The arrows of the jets then give a third direction in space.

Wang has compared the assembly to a three-dimensional puzzle. Each observation added a piece. Orbit, disks, and jets eventually belonged to one picture. Ruben Fedriani of the Institute of Astrophysics of Andalusia and Jonathan C. Tan, a professor at Chalmers University of Technology and the University of Virginia, are among the coauthors. A continuum image at 0.9 millimetres shows the binary at the centre, with a reconstructed orbit drawn through it.

## Why a shared disk has trouble here

Two geometric facts do the arguing. The orbit has a large eccentricity. It is a distorted, stretched path, not a near-circle. And each circumstellar disk is strongly tilted relative to the other disk and relative to the orbital plane.

A single gas disk that fragments should leave a memory. The stars and their disks inherit roughly the same spin axis, the angular momentum of the parent disk. The measured arrangement does not look like that memory. The team's reading is that the two stars formed independently, met at close range while they were still growing inside the molecular cloud, and became gravitationally bound. Tan's way of putting the early stage: it is complicated, and stars that were born apart can still meet and end up bound.

That reading is a comparative fit. Nobody filmed the flyby. The together-from-birth model has trouble with the tilts and the stretched orbit. The encounter model has less trouble. The capture, if recent, also explains why the orbit is still eccentric. Tides and leftover gas can circularize an orbit later. A still-elongated path is a clue that this rounding has not finished.

## One system is a route, not a census

Nothing here says most massive binaries formed by capture. It says this one is difficult to file under co-formation in a single disk, and that a near-parabolic encounter can assemble a massive protobinary. A rate would need many systems. The same technique can be pointed at other young, cloud-buried pairs. Earlier work could measure an on-sky separation, and only rarely a line-of-sight velocity difference. A long, precise campaign can now recover the three-dimensional layout. Future observations should tighten the orbit of IRAS 07299-1651 itself. A sample of orbits would test whether this route is common or rare. The result is a way into the binary. Planets are outside the claim.

Read the Nature Astronomy article for the orbit solutions and the disk angles. Read the ALMA release for the observatory's version of the same campaign. The geometry is the measurement. Separate births plus a close gravitational meeting are the history the team prefers.

### Moving sodium in PDS 70 may be comets carrying water inward

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-07_planet-formation_pds70-exocomets-water/
- Published: 2026-09-07
- Topics: [Planet Formation](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/planet-formation/)
- Freshness context: Published in Nature Communications on 24 August 2026.
- Summary: PDS 70, a planetary system just over five million years old and about 370 light-years away, already holds at least two gas giants. Lund University astronomers report sodium gas that appears and disappears in front of the star, a pattern consistent with icy bodies heating up and venting. Simulations show those giants can fling outer comets inward, a possible water route while planets are still forming.
- Why it matters: Earth's water source is still an open question, with water-rich asteroids and comets both in the running. PDS 70 lets astronomers watch a young system, slightly cooler than the Sun, where inward-scattered ice could deliver water to the planet-forming region. The sodium signal is evidence of exocomets, not a measurement of how much water arrived.
- Suggested next question: Compare the comet and asteroid routes proposed for Earth's water, and ask what a still-forming system can and cannot decide about that history.
- Explore further: [Nature Communications: Potential sublimating exocomets around the young star PDS 70](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-76880-y)
- Sources:
  - [Nature Communications](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-76880-y)
  - [Lund University](https://www.lunduniversity.lu.se/article/comets-may-have-transported-water-young-planetary-system)

Fuller note:

## A young system, a moving wisp of sodium

PDS 70 is just over five million years old and lies around 370 light-years from Earth. The star is slightly cooler than the Sun. At least two gas giants already orbit inside the system, still in the era when planets and leftover debris share the same disk. Astronomers at Lund University report evidence of exocomets there: comets in another planetary system. The paper, in Nature Communications on 24 August 2026, carries a careful title. Potential sublimating exocomets around the young star PDS 70. "Potential" is doing real work.

The clue is sodium. The team analysed observations from 2018 and found sodium gas moving at several kilometres per second relative to the star. The gas appears and disappears over several nights. That pattern matches what you would expect if small bodies were crossing the line of sight, heating up, and venting. The star is the lamp. The sodium is a temporary filter in front of it.

When a comet swings close to its star, ice on the surface turns straight into gas. That skip of the liquid stage is sublimation. The gas can imprint on the starlight for a while, then leave the beam as the body moves on. Aline Novais, an astronomy researcher at Lund, describes the variations as a sign that comets may be passing through the inner parts of the system.

## What would count as a comet you cannot photograph

An exocomet is almost never a resolved rock. At 370 light-years the nucleus is a point you do not see. You see chemistry that shows up, shifts in velocity, and fades. Several kilometres per second is a speed that fits gas leaving a small body on a star-crossing path, not a static cloud parked in the disk. Several nights is a short clock. Disk gas can vary too, so the team is arguing from a pattern, not from a portrait of a nucleus.

Novais also places the claim in context. This is the first time there is evidence of exocomets around a star that is relatively cool, much like the Sun. This is also the youngest system in which exocomet activity has been proposed. Young and Sun-like is why PDS 70 keeps coming up in planet-formation work. You can watch a system that still resembles an early stage of our own, with giant planets already on the scene.

Water vapour was detected near the star as early as 2023. That earlier detection is a neighbouring fact, not the same measurement as the 2018 sodium. Vapour says water molecules are present in the inner system. The sodium variations are the new argument that icy bodies are crossing and venting. Keep them in separate columns. One is a chemical presence. The other is a time-varying signature the team ties to comets.

## The giants as a gravitational sling

The second half of the Lund account is a simulation, and it should stay in its own column. The researchers computed comet orbits under the pull of the gas giants. Objects far out in the system can be tugged and flung toward the star. Comets form in the cold outer regions, where water can exist as ice and other volatile substances stay frozen. Send those bodies inward and they can carry water and those volatiles into the region where planets form.

Alexandra Stockwell Murphy, an astronomer at Lund, compares that path to a possible process in the early Solar System, in which comets may have helped deliver water to the young Earth. The comparison is a resemblance. It is not a solved ledger for Earth's oceans. Where Earth's water came from remains an open question. Water-rich asteroids and comets are both possible sources. PDS 70 offers a look at a similar traffic pattern while a planetary system is still young.

A simulation that shows an open path is evidence the path can operate. It is not a measurement of how much water moved, how often the scattering happens, or whether any rocky world in the system has already collected an ocean. The paper does not claim oceans. Lund's headline is about transport that may have happened. "May" matches the sodium evidence, which is a sign, and the orbits, which are a capability.

## What the next telescope is being asked to do

Jens Hoeijmakers, an astronomy researcher at Lund, points to the Extremely Large Telescope now being built in Chile. In the coming years it should be able to ask whether further planets sit in the system, and to sharpen the picture of how water and other planet-building materials move. That is a future observation. It is not a result in hand.

Until then the split inside this note is the part worth keeping. Observation: sodium gas from 2018, moving at several kilometres per second, present on some nights and gone on others, read as potential sublimating exocomets around a star a little cooler than the Sun. Context: water vapour seen near the star by 2023, and at least two gas giants in a system just over five million years old. Interpretation: those giants can scatter outer icy bodies inward, so comets are a plausible courier for water. The Nature Communications article is the authority for the signatures. Lund's article is the secondary explanation. Neither one has weighed the delivered water.

### One odd event in a xenon tank, and nobody is calling it dark matter

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-06_fundamental-physics_lz-dark-matter-candidate/
- Published: 2026-09-06
- Topics: [Gravity & Fundamental Physics](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/gravity-and-fundamental-physics/)
- Freshness context: Announced by the LUX-ZEPLIN collaboration and Berkeley Lab on 1 September 2026.
- Summary: LUX-ZEPLIN recorded one particle interaction that known backgrounds struggle to explain. The detector holds 10 tonnes of liquid xenon nearly a mile underground in South Dakota, and this search used 220 live days from March 2023 through April 2024. The outlier is a 2.6 sigma hint, far short of the 5 sigma line for a discovery. The collaboration is not claiming dark matter.
- Why it matters: Dark matter is about 85 percent of the mass of the universe, inferred from gravity, with no confirmed particle yet. A single xenon event can start a search. It cannot finish one. More events in the same high-energy corner, or a background that accounts for this one, will decide whether the hint survives.
- Suggested next question: Ask how galaxy motions and gravitational lensing reveal dark matter's gravity while the particle itself stays unidentified.
- Explore further: [LUX-ZEPLIN: new high-energy dark-matter search result](https://lz.lbl.gov/)
- Sources:
  - [LUX-ZEPLIN Collaboration](https://lz.lbl.gov/)
  - [Berkeley Lab](https://newscenter.lbl.gov/2026/09/01/lz-sees-surprising-result-in-search-for-dark-matter/)
  - [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/science/scientists-make-potential-breakthrough-search-dark-matter-2026-09-01/)

Fuller note:

## One interaction, parked short of a discovery

LUX-ZEPLIN recorded a single particle interaction that is hard to explain with the backgrounds the collaboration knows how to model. It landed in a part of the data where a dark-matter particle could show up, and where ordinary mimics are supposed to be scarce. The collaboration is not calling it a detection.

Rick Gaitskell, a professor at Brown University and the LZ spokesperson, has been plain about the mood. Intrigued. Unwilling to get ahead of one event. Not claiming to have seen dark matter. The analysis was presented at the 2026 TeV Particle Astrophysics conference in Japan. A paper is headed to arXiv and to Physical Review Letters. Berkeley Lab's write-up of 1 September 2026, and the collaboration's own site, carry the details. Reuters reported the announcement the same day. Once the journal article is public, it is the authority for the energy, the cuts, and the background model.

The experiment sits nearly a mile underground at the Sanford Underground Research Facility in South Dakota. Berkeley Lab manages it. About 250 scientists from 39 institutions work on it. The detector holds 10 tonnes of ultrapure liquid xenon. It is built to look for WIMPs, weakly interacting massive particles, one long-standing guess for what dark matter might be. Dark matter remains a gravitational fact, about 85 percent of the mass of the universe, and an unidentified substance. Nobody has a confirmed particle.

## Same 220 days, a different slice of energy

The exposure is 220 live days, from March 2023 through April 2024. An earlier search of that same dataset hunted the faintest, simplest WIMP scatters, the kind that deposit very little energy. This analysis opened another slice: interactions that could deposit more energy. Sam Eriksen of the University of Bristol is the lead author.

A WIMP, if that is the right family at all, would bump a xenon nucleus and then leave. The bump deposits energy, and the xenon records it as a flash. Most flashes in a laboratory have duller origins: leftover radioactivity in the materials, neutrons born in the surrounding rock, cosmic rays that still punch through. A mile of rock cuts the cosmic-ray rate sharply. The analysis then throws out events that look like the remaining mimics. The search region is quiet enough that one survivor is news. It is not quiet enough, with this exposure, to name the survivor.

LZ expects genuine dark-matter events to be extremely rare. Several matching events could become a first detection. One event is a hint. That difference is the whole argument against a victory lap.

## What 2.6 sigma is allowed to mean

The statistical weight is 2.6 sigma. In this analysis that corresponds to about a 0.5 percent chance that known backgrounds explain the event. Five sigma is the usual discovery line in this field. The gap between 2.6 and 5 is wide. A 0.5 percent chance is uncommon. It is still well short of a discovery.

If the event were a WIMP, the collaboration's reading puts the mass likely at or above 200 GeV/c2, more than 200 times the mass of a proton, and points to a less simple interaction than the baseline model. The "if" matters. The fact on the table is one outlier that survived the checks they know how to run. The mass and the interaction type are a conditional reading of that outlier, not a weighed particle.

Aaron Manalaysay at Berkeley Lab, chair of LZ's Institutional Board, has said a rare background the team has not thought of remains possible. He has also called this the first outlier in his experiments that still looks valid after a long look. Both can be true. An event can survive the known backgrounds and still be something ordinary that the model missed.

## The dataset is large, and the run is not over

LZ already holds the largest dark-matter dataset of this kind, and the detector is still running. More live days will either grow this hint, with more events in the same corner, or wash it out as a one-off. Until that happens, the honest summary is Gaitskell's. Something in the xenon is interesting. Dark matter has not been identified.

A useful habit, if you follow the next paper: separate the count from the story. The count is one event, 220 days, 2.6 sigma, about a 0.5 percent chance under known backgrounds, a xenon mass of 10 tonnes. The story, still optional, is a heavy WIMP with a less simple interaction. Optional stories are how this field stays honest while the tank keeps taking data.

### The universe is making fewer stars, and the hydrogen is still there

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-05_galaxy-evolution_star-formation-hydrogen/
- Published: 2026-09-05
- Topics: [Galaxies & Galactic Evolution](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/galaxies-and-galactic-evolution/)
- Freshness context: Published in Nature Astronomy on 1 September 2026.
- Summary: FAST and DESI, used together on about 2.5 million galaxies across nearly one-third of the sky, find that the cosmic star formation rate was 2.46 times higher 4.5 billion years ago than it is today. The Chinese Academy of Sciences summary rounds that factor to about 2.5. Neutral atomic hydrogen, measured with the 21-centimetre line, was only about 1.4 times denser then. The mismatch points away from an empty fuel tank.
- Why it matters: A fading star formation rate is often blamed on galaxies running out of gas. Here the atomic hydrogen thinned only modestly while star formation fell by a much larger factor. The useful next question is how galaxies turn atomic hydrogen into the molecular gas that actually forms stars, and why that step grew less efficient as gas from the cosmic web thinned.
- Suggested next question: Follow the path from atomic hydrogen in the cosmic web to molecular clouds, and ask which step stalls when star formation slows.
- Explore further: [Nature Astronomy: Weak evolution of cosmic atomic hydrogen over the past 4.5 billion years](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41550-026-02965-9)
- Sources:
  - [Nature Astronomy](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41550-026-02965-9)
  - [Chinese Academy of Sciences / EurekAlert](https://e3.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1142061)

Fuller note:

## The factory slowed. The tank barely did.

Stars do not form from the hydrogen you can count most easily. They form from molecular hydrogen, two atoms bound together, inside cold dense clouds. The larger stockpile is neutral atomic hydrogen, a single atom with its electron still attached. Astronomers abbreviate that gas as HI. It is the intermediate reservoir: gathered into a galaxy, not yet a molecule, not yet a star.

A Nature Astronomy paper published on 1 September 2026 puts two clocks side by side over the past 4.5 billion years. Star formation was faster in the past. The paper's figure is a factor of 2.46. The cosmic star formation rate 4.5 billion years ago was about 2.46 times the rate today. The Chinese Academy of Sciences summary, distributed through EurekAlert, rounds that same change to about 2.5 times. The precise factor belongs to the paper. The round number belongs to the CAS account. Name the source, and the two wordings describe the same drop.

Neutral atomic hydrogen refused to follow the same drop. Its density 4.5 billion years ago was only about 1.4 times the density today. That pairing is the measurement. A star factory slowed by more than a factor of two. The atomic tank thinned by a much smaller factor.

## A faint line, stacked across a third of the sky

HI announces itself with radio light at a wavelength of 21 centimetres. The line is faint. A single distant galaxy rarely delivers a clean detection on its own. The team used spectral stacking. Take many galaxies whose distances are already known, shift each spectrum so the expected line lands in the same channel, and add them. Noise averages down. The mean HI signal comes up.

The distances come from DESI, the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument, which supplies the redshifts. The radio spectra come from FAST, China's large radio telescope. Together the datasets cover about 2.5 million galaxies and nearly one-third of the sky. The institutions leading the work are the National Astronomical Observatories of China, the Shanghai Astronomical Observatory, and Shanghai Jiao Tong University, with DESI collaborators.

Stacking is built for an average. It will not name the cloud in a particular spiral that failed to collapse. It will say that, across a huge slice of the recent universe, newborn stars and atomic gas parted company. The journal article, DOI 10.1038/s41550-026-02965-9, is the place to read both curves. The CAS summary is the institutional account of the same result.

## The empty-tank story does not fit the gas

For years a simple story traveled with the fading of cosmic starlight. Galaxies used up their fuel. If depletion were the whole tale, the HI reservoir should have fallen about as hard as the star formation rate. It did not. The gas is still there, in the limited sense that its density changed far less than the rate at which stars were being made.

The team's interpretation is a different sentence, and it should stay labeled as an interpretation. This is not a simple fuel crisis. Conversion of HI into molecular hydrogen became less efficient. Two changes sit under that reading. Supply from the cosmic web weakened, so less fresh gas streamed in from outside galaxies. Gas density fell, and lower density makes it harder for atoms to meet, stick, and become H2.

Think of a kitchen. The pantry is only a little emptier than it was. The meals coming out have fallen by the paper's factor of 2.46. The slow step is the cooking. The shelf still holds flour. Molecular hydrogen is the ingredient that actually collapses into stars. HI is that flour, still sitting on the counter.

## What these factors will not decide

Nothing in the stack measures one disk's turbulence, one black hole's push, or one bar stirring a single galaxy. Hot halos, stellar feedback, and messy orbits can all change how fast atomic gas becomes molecular. Those are local ways the same bottleneck can appear. This survey averages them into one cosmic trend.

Keep the numbers glued to the right curves. The factor 2.46, or about 2.5 in the CAS wording, describes star formation. About 1.4 describes the HI density. Swap them and you invent either a crisis or a surplus the data do not show.

A last distinction is small enough to carry around. The 21-centimetre line counts atomic hydrogen. Star formation counts what happened after that gas became molecular and collapsed. A universe with a large HI reservoir can still look quiet in starlight, if the step between the atom and the molecule has grown clumsy. The paper measures the two trends. The efficiency story is how the team reads the gap between them.

### Hubble watches a ten-sided wave grow at Saturn's south pole

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-04_solar-system_saturn-south-pole-decagon/
- Published: 2026-09-04
- Topics: [Solar System & Planetary Science](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/solar-system-and-planetary-science/)
- Freshness context: Published in Science Advances on 2 September 2026.
- Summary: Hubble and ground-based images show a giant ten-sided wave around Saturn's south pole, the first large regular jet polygon in the southern hemisphere. Faint signs are in data from 2023 and 2024. By 2025 the shape was much clearer. The northern hexagon has lasted more than 40 years. This southern wave appears to be strengthening, so observers may be watching one form.
- Why it matters: Saturn's north polar hexagon is a long-lived jet. The southern decagon looks younger and still changing. Watching it grow could show how a jet locks into a polygon, why the planet makes these shapes, and whether a new one can last. The cause and the lifetime are still open.
- Suggested next question: Look at Saturn's north polar hexagon, a six-sided jet that has held its shape for more than 40 years, and compare that longevity with a southern wave that is still growing.
- Explore further: [Science Advances: a decagon at Saturn's south pole](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aee4251)
- Sources:
  - [Science Advances](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aee4251)
  - [NASA Hubble](https://science.nasa.gov/missions/hubble/nasas-hubble-tracks-new-decagon-encircling-saturns-south-pole/)
  - [University of Leicester](https://le.ac.uk/news/2026/august/observations-mysterious-shape-saturn-clouds)

Fuller note:

## A ten-sided wave that was faint, then obvious

Hubble has caught a giant decagonal wave around Saturn's south pole. A decagon is a ten-sided shape. This is the first large, regular-sided jet pattern seen in the planet's southern hemisphere. Faint signs are in data from 2023 and 2024. By 2025 the shape was much clearer. The analysis is in Science Advances, 2 September 2026.

Saturn's north polar hexagon, a six-sided jet, has been there every time observers have looked, for more than 40 years. Amy Simon, co-author and principal investigator of Hubble's Outer Planet Atmospheres Legacy program at NASA Goddard, says the southern feature is different. It appears to be strengthening. OPAL has photographed the outer planets once a year for more than a decade, which is why a slow pattern can be caught while it grows instead of as a single postcard.

The south pole has also been hard to see. Saturn's seasons tipped it back into view from Earth. That geometry is the reason a structure of this size could sit unnoticed and then, over a few years, become obvious.

## Ground observers first, Hubble for the earlier years

Agustín Sánchez-Lavega, at the University of the Basque Country, leads the study. The university runs the Planetary Virtual Observatory Laboratory, a site that collects ground-based images of solar-system planets from observers around the world. In 2024 images contributed there, Sánchez-Lavega and amateur astronomers Trevor Barry and Jean-Paul Oger noticed a subtle undulating band along the southern pole. Ground images from 2025 pushed harder toward a ten-sided shape.

Hubble then did something the discovery year alone could not. Its view from space stays sharp across a full rotation of Saturn, without smearing by Earth's atmosphere. The OPAL frames confirmed the feature was already present in 2023. So the wave did not appear out of nowhere in the year the ground observers named it. It was weak, then clearer.

Sánchez-Lavega's group had been looking for a southern counterpart of the hexagon in Hubble images since 1990. Saturn's north-south jet system is roughly symmetric, so a polygon in the north made a polygon in the south a reasonable thing to hunt. Cassini, in orbit from 2004 to 2017, showed no long-lived southern polygon. The absence in that earlier record is part of why Simon's question bites: this seems to have formed recently, and nobody knows why it formed now.

## Not a stain on the cloud tops

The wave sits in one of Saturn's jet streams and extends through several layers of the atmosphere. Different Hubble filters look at different altitudes, because different wavelengths of light escape from different depths. The apparent position of the decagon shifts slightly between those filters. That shift is evidence the structure is vertically extended, not a mark painted on the cloud tops.

A jet can prefer a polygon over a circle when the wind's speed changes sharply with latitude and the waves that fit inside that shear lock into a standing pattern, a shape that holds still relative to the planet. The number of sides is set by how those waves fit. The hexagon is the textbook case of that idea. A decagon would be a different number of sides in a different jet, possibly a younger one.

Copying the hexagon's explanation onto the south pole is the temptation. The data so far justify the geometry, the vertical reach, and the fact that the pattern is growing. They do not yet show that the same fluid mechanics produced both shapes, or that the southern wave will last for decades the way the northern one has. That reading is an interpretation. The authors want more Hubble time, JWST, and computer models before they will say how the decagon formed, how long it may last, or how it compares with the north.

## What a long watch is for

Mike Wong, a co-author at the University of California, Berkeley, notes that OPAL's finds tend to come from the stack of years, not from one visit. This decagon is that kind of find. The team plans to keep observing, to see whether the wave settles into a long-lived, stable configuration like the northern hexagon or keeps changing. Later images could also speak to what drives the wave, and to how giant-planet weather compares with the storms we watch on Earth. Those are hopes for the next data, not results from this one.

Measured, then: a ten-sided wave, multi-layered, emerging across 2023, 2024, and 2025, the first large regular polygon in the south. Still open: the cause, the lifetime, and the family resemblance to the hexagon. Science Advances, DOI 10.1126/sciadv.aee4251, carries the analysis. NASA's Hubble write-up is the public account. The next useful comparison is the northern hexagon itself, a jet that chose a shape and then kept it, which this southern wave has not yet had time to do.

### Faint stars may hide extra mass in early massive galaxies

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-03_galaxy-evolution_hidden-mass-early-galaxies/
- Published: 2026-09-03
- Topics: [Galaxies & Galactic Evolution](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/galaxies-and-galactic-evolution/); [Stars & Stellar Evolution](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/stars-and-stellar-evolution/)
- Freshness context: Published in Nature Astronomy on 21 August 2026.
- Summary: JWST and Very Large Telescope spectra of nine massive quiescent galaxies at a redshift of about 0.7 show excess low-mass stars in the most massive systems. The oldest, with stars formed at a redshift above 5, has the most bottom-heavy initial mass function. If similar mixes applied to their early ancestors, some galaxy masses could rise by a factor of about 4, give or take about 1.
- Why it matters: Galaxy masses at large distances assume a Milky Way mix of stellar birth masses. These spectra suggest that mix fails for the biggest quiescent systems. If the early galaxies JWST has been finding inherited the same excess of faint stars, models must assemble even more mass in less time.
- Suggested next question: Look at the initial mass function, the distribution of stellar birth masses used to turn a galaxy's light into a stellar mass.
- Explore further: [Nature Astronomy: hidden mass and bottom-heavy stellar mixes](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41550-026-02932-4)
- Sources:
  - [Nature Astronomy](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41550-026-02932-4)
  - [Penn State](https://pure.psu.edu/en/publications/hidden-mass-in-early-galaxies-revealed-by-bottom-heavy-initial-ma/)

Fuller note:

## The mass you infer from the light

A galaxy's stellar mass is usually inferred, not weighed. You see light. You assume a mix of bright stars and faint ones, then scale up. That mix is the initial mass function, the IMF: the distribution of masses stars have at birth. High-mass stars dominate the light and die young. Low-mass stars are faint, live a long time, and hold most of the mass. If the mix is bottom-heavy, with more faint stars than the standard assumption, the same glow hides more mass.

Distant galaxies are usually assigned an IMF like the Milky Way's. The faint stars are not seen one by one. Their contribution is an extrapolation. Change the extrapolation and the mass changes, even if the spectrum you measured stays the same. JWST has been finding massive galaxies that formed and evolved faster than galaxy-formation models predicted. Many had already assembled a large mass in stars about 12 billion years ago. Those masses are only as firm as the IMF that was assumed.

A Nature Astronomy paper published on 21 August 2026 goes after that assumption with full-spectrum models, fits to the whole spectrum rather than to one or two features. The title is "Hidden mass in early galaxies revealed by bottom-heavy initial mass functions."

## Nine quiet galaxies, not the frantic ones

The spectra are of nine massive quiescent galaxies at a redshift of about 0.7. Quiescent means star formation has largely shut down, so a fresh burst of short-lived bright stars is not dominating the light. Redshift is the stretch of light by cosmic expansion. A larger number means the light has traveled longer, and we see the galaxy further back in time. About 0.7 is not the early universe itself. It is a later, quieter view of galaxies whose stars may have formed much earlier.

The JWST spectra come from a program called the Initial Mass Function of Early Red NIRSpec Objects. NIRSpec is JWST's near-infrared spectrograph. Those data were extended to bluer wavelengths with deep spectra from the Very Large Telescope's Large Early Galaxy Astrophysics Census. The combination is what let the authors ask about low-mass stars instead of adopting the Milky Way's mix and moving on.

The measurement claim is specific. The most massive galaxies in the nine have an excess of low-mass stars. The oldest galaxy in the sample, with a formation redshift greater than 5, has the most bottom-heavy IMF. Formation redshift is the epoch the stars are estimated to have formed, which can be earlier than the epoch at which we happen to observe the galaxy. We see this one at about 0.7, after it has gone quiet. Its stars, on the team's fit, formed when redshift was still above 5.

## The factor of about four is a maybe

The striking number is conditional. This oldest galaxy may be a descendant of the galaxies JWST has been calling "impossibly early." If those ancestors had a similarly bottom-heavy IMF, their stellar masses would rise by a factor of approximately 4, with an uncertainty of about 1. The paper says that increase may amplify the tension with galaxy-formation models.

That reading is an interpretation. The spectra in hand are the nine quiescent galaxies. The early, still-forming systems are a different set. Carrying a bottom-heavy IMF backward, along a possible family line from a redshift above 5 to the "impossibly early" population, is an inference. "May be a descendant" is the paper's wording, and the "may" is doing real work. It is not a statement that these nine galaxies have been reweighed by a factor of four.

If the inference holds, the formation problem gets worse, not easier. Adding hidden low-mass stars raises the mass that had to be assembled in a short time. Models that were already strained by heavy early galaxies would be more strained. That is why a result on nine quieter systems still lands on the early universe. It does not land there as a finished census.

## Where the assumption usually hides

The standard conversion from light to mass is good enough for a lot of nearby galaxies, which is why it became the default. It fails quietly. Two galaxies with the same brightness can differ in mass if one is full of faint red stars and the other is not. Star-formation history, chemical pattern, and the light from the giants all get folded into the fit. A bottom-heavy function changes how much mass you assign to the stars you cannot see.

Nothing here says every early galaxy is bottom-heavy. The claim is aimed at the most massive of these quiescent systems, and then, more tentatively, at their possible ancestors. The route is stellar populations, the light of the stars, not a dynamical weighing by orbital speeds. A dynamical mass, if you had one, would have to be shared among stars, gas, and dark matter. This paper does not make that split. It says the stellar piece may be larger than the Milky Way recipe implied.

Treat the Nature Astronomy paper, DOI 10.1038/s41550-026-02932-4, as the authority for the spectral fits. The Penn State record carries the same abstract. The factor-of-four statement belongs in the conditional column until those ancestor galaxies are measured the same way. The useful next step is the IMF itself: the table of birth masses that turns a spectrum into a mass. Change the table, and a generation of early-galaxy masses moves with it.

### JWST watches planet-forming disks lose their gas

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-02_planet-formation_jwst-disk-winds/
- Published: 2026-09-02
- Topics: [Planet Formation](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/planet-formation/)
- Freshness context: Published online in The Astronomical Journal on 25 August 2026.
- Summary: Archival JWST spectra of 72 young Sun-like stars show gas leaving their planet-forming disks. Extended molecular hydrogen and ionized neon appear in 66 of 72 disks, conical hydrogen winds in 46, and fast neon jets in 40. Young, strongly accreting systems favor jets and mixed winds. Older, weaker accretors favor atomic winds, which the team ties to photoevaporation.
- Why it matters: Giant planets need a large gas supply, and disks do not keep that gas forever. Across 72 young stars, the way gas leaves shifts from jets and molecular winds toward atomic winds as accretion fades. That sequence is a physical ordering. How much gas leaves, and from where in the disk, is still unmeasured.
- Suggested next question: Look at photoevaporation, the heating of a planet-forming disk by ultraviolet light and X-rays until the gas can escape the star.
- Explore further: [SETI Institute: JWST and disappearing disk gas](https://www.seti.org/news/jwst-reveals-a-race-against-time/)
- Sources:
  - [SETI Institute](https://www.seti.org/news/jwst-reveals-a-race-against-time/)
  - [The Astronomical Journal](https://doi.org/10.3847/1538-3881/ae9089)

Fuller note:

## Seventy-two disks, counted one by one

The gas that can build a Jupiter does not sit still. It leaves. A paper in The Astronomical Journal, online on 25 August 2026, uses archival spectra from JWST's Mid-Infrared Instrument to watch how it leaves. The instrument, MIRI, spreads infrared light into a spectrum so particular molecules and ions show up as distinct lines. Naman S. Bajaj of the University of Arizona led the work. Ilaria Pascucci is the second author. Uma Gorti of the SETI Institute and NASA Ames is a co-author. The title is "JWST/MIRI Reveals the Evolution from Molecular to Atomic Disk Winds." The DOI is 10.3847/1538-3881/ae9089.

The sample is 72 young Sun-like stars. Each disk is one age and one accretion rate. Accretion, here, means gas from the disk is still falling onto the star. Lined up, the 72 systems are frames in a sequence rather than 72 unrelated snapshots. That is the useful part. A single disk is a portrait. A row of them, sorted by how hard the star is still being fed, starts to look like a timeline.

What they actually counted: extended molecular hydrogen and ionized neon in 66 of the 72 disks. Conical molecular-hydrogen winds in 46. Fast neon jets in 40. Every system with a neon jet also showed a wind traced by molecular hydrogen or oxygen. Those are the census numbers. Ionized neon means neon atoms that have lost electrons, a sign the gas is hot and energetic. A conical wind is gas leaving in a cone that opens away from the star, rather than a spherical puff.
