## Jets first, then a warmer way out

In the young systems that are still accreting, the spectra show strong jets and broad winds that carry both molecules and atoms. The picture the team favors is magnetic. A magnetic field threaded through the disk can lift gas along the field lines and carry angular momentum away with it. Angular momentum is the spin that keeps disk gas from falling straight in. Remove some of that spin, and other gas can move inward onto the star, while the wind itself leaves the system. The disk keeps feeding the star, and it also loses mass.

Later, when less material is falling in, the jets weaken. The remaining wind is mostly atomic. High-energy light from the star can get through the thinning gas, heat the upper layers of the disk, and drive them off. That heating-and-escape route is photoevaporation. Ultraviolet light and X-rays do the heating. The gas does not need a magnetic slingshot anymore. It is simply warm enough to flow away into space.

The paper's ordering is young and strongly accreting on one side, older and weakly accreting on the other. Strong jets and mixed molecular-plus-atomic winds sit with the first group, and the team reads them as magnetic driving. Mostly atomic winds sit with the second group, and the team reads those as photoevaporation taking over. That reading is an interpretation of which force dominates. The spectra show which lines are there, and how the mix changes along the sequence. They do not come with a label that says "magnetic" or "ultraviolet" printed on the gas.

## A prediction that waited for molecular hydrogen

In 2020, before JWST could trace molecular hydrogen directly, a study led by Pascucci's team predicted that molecular winds would be present early, and that they could be massive enough to block X-rays. If the inner wind is thick with molecules, X-rays from the star have a harder time reaching the disk beyond. Tracing H2, the hydrogen molecule, is what let this sample check that prediction. The molecules are there, in the young systems, in the numbers above. The prediction held in that sense: JWST sees the molecular wind the earlier work had expected, by measuring H2 itself rather than inferring it.

A 2024 image of gas leaving the disk around the star T Cha, from the same group, had already shown that these instruments could do the job for one system. Seventy-two stars is what turns a portrait into a trend. The cones, the jets, and the handoff from molecules to atoms are the trend.

## The amount of gas, and where it leaves, are still open

Disk dispersal sets a deadline. Once the gas is gone, the chance to build a gas-rich planet is over. A gas giant has to assemble its atmosphere while the disk can still supply it. Our own Jupiter is the local reminder of the stakes. The JWST sample is a look at other stars while that supply is leaving, sorted by age and by how strongly they are still accreting.

The paper does not say how much gas each wind removes, or which radius in the disk the gas comes from. Bajaj's group lists that as the next measurement. Without those numbers, the change in mechanism is visible and the timetable is not. "Race against time" describes the stakes. It does not name a schedule.

The Astronomical Journal paper is the place to check the line measurements. The SETI Institute write-up is the secondary account used here. The next useful question is photoevaporation in detail: how ultraviolet and X-ray photons heat a disk until the gas can leave, and how that route compares with a wind that is still mostly molecular.

### MoM-BH*-1 looks like a star powered by a buried black hole

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-01_cosmic-dawn_black-hole-star-mom-bh-1/
- Published: 2026-09-01
- Topics: [Black Holes](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/black-holes/); [Cosmology & Early Universe](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/cosmology-and-early-universe/)
- Freshness context: Published in Nature on 12 August 2026. The freshness window was widened past 15 days because this peer-reviewed result was more distinct than fresher mission items.
- Summary: JWST's MoM survey found MoM-BH*-1, an extremely red object seen about 660 million years after the Big Bang. It shows the deepest Balmer break yet, almost no metals, and about 100 billion times more energy than fusion in a known star can produce. The best-matching model is a black hole of about 100,000 solar masses inside a hydrogen cocoon the size of the Solar System.
- Why it matters: Giant black holes already exist very early, and how they grew is still open. MoM-BH*-1 is a spectrum fusion cannot power, fit by a black hole wrapped in dense hydrogen. If little red dots, common in JWST images and mostly gone today, are the same kind of object, early black-hole masses may need another look.
- Suggested next question: Look at JWST's little red dots and at how a deep Balmer break can come from dense hydrogen rather than from ordinary starlight.
- Explore further: [Nature: a gas-enshrouded black hole at cosmic dawn](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-10846-4)
- Sources:
  - [Nature](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-10846-4)
  - [MIT News](https://news.mit.edu/2026/astronomers-discover-brand-new-type-astrophysical-object-black-hole-star-0812)

Fuller note:

## Too bright to be a star, too clean to be a dusty galaxy

JWST found an exceptionally red source the team calls MoM-BH*-1. It is seen about 660 million years after the Big Bang, a few hundred million years into cosmic history. The spectrum is the awkward part. It shows an unusually deep Balmer break and broad hydrogen features. A Balmer break is a sharp drop in the light on the blue side of certain wavelengths. Ordinary stellar atmospheres make one. Vega, a bright star in the night sky, shows the familiar version. The break in MoM-BH*-1 is the deepest yet seen in anything, which is hard to square with a normal star.

There is a second oddity. The light is almost pure hydrogen and helium. Metals, the astronomer's word for anything heavier, are nearly absent. And the object is violently bright. It puts out about 100 billion times more energy than any known star can produce by nuclear fusion. Energies like that are routine for a feeding black hole. They are not routine for a star. The object also looks, in size, like a star on the scale of the Solar System. Fusion still cannot power the glow.

The paper is in Nature, 12 August 2026, led by Rohan Naidu and colleagues. Naidu is a NASA Hubble Fellow and Pappalardo Fellow at MIT's Kavli Institute. Co-authors include Robert Simcoe and Wendy Sun. They were not hunting a new kind of object. The survey is called Mirage or Miracle, MoM for short, and it was aimed at the earliest galaxies. Naidu's line on that search is worth keeping: some of what looks like an extremely bright early galaxy, a "miracle," may be a mirage.

## Dust was the obvious guess. The spectrum refused it.

Very red usually means dust. Smoke reddens a sunset. Dust reddens a galaxy. Simcoe says the other signatures did not match a dust screen. The team asked a narrower question: can hydrogen alone, with no dust, make something this red? Their simulations said yes, if the hydrogen is packed so densely that it behaves more like the surface of an enormous star than like a thin cloud of gas.

A photosphere is the visible surface of a star, the layer where light last scatters before it escapes. A pseudo-photosphere is a cocoon of gas doing that job without being a star. In the simulations, a dense hydrogen screen soaks up blue light and produces a deep Balmer break. It also hides the problem of missing metals if there are hardly any metals to begin with. It does not, by itself, explain the brightness. Fusion still cannot power it.

So they put an accreting black hole in the middle of the hydrogen and varied the mass until the fake spectrum sat near the real one. Accreting means gas is falling in, heating, and radiating. The black hole does the job fusion would do in a star. The gas supplies the fake surface.

## The fit, and what is still a model

The best match, in the paper's interpretation and in Naidu's description, is a central black hole of about 100,000 times the Sun's mass, wrapped in a turbulent, dust-free hydrogen envelope roughly the size of the Solar System. The object looks star-like. The engine is not a star. They named it MoM-BH*-1: the survey, plus "black hole star, one."

That reading is an interpretation. The observation is the red, metal-poor spectrum, the extreme Balmer break, the broad hydrogen lines, and a luminosity fusion cannot supply. The black-hole-plus-cocoon arrangement is the scenario that matched the simulations. It is not a photograph of the interior. A different engine that somehow produced the same spectrum is not ruled out by a fit alone. The fit is the reason this picture is the one they prefer.

MoM-BH*-1 outshines its host galaxy, so the light is nearly pure "black hole star" light. That is what makes this object easier to read than a blend of galaxy and central source. The host is still there. It is just not the thing you are mostly seeing.

## Little red dots, and a claim that stays a claim

Little red dots are common in JWST images, and they are mostly gone by the present day. The team suspects MoM-BH*-1 is the first clear member of a class. Naidu argues that every little red dot is consistent with a black hole star sitting inside an ordinary early galaxy, and that this object is special because the central source dominates the light. "Consistent with" is not "shown to be." The dots are fainter than MoM-BH*-1. Their light is harder to separate from the galaxy around them.

If the same model is later used to weigh those dots, estimates of early black-hole masses could move, and so could the story of how the first galaxies grew. A buried black hole can gain mass quickly if the gas around it is dense, which is why this picture is attractive to people trying to understand giant black holes that already exist early on. That revision is a possible consequence. It is not yet a required one.

The Nature paper is the authority for the spectral measurements and the model grid. MIT's write-up is a clear secondary account of the same work. Both leave the little-red-dot population as an argument, which is the right size for the claim.

### Roman launches toward L2 to survey the dark universe

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-08-31_space-observatory_roman-launches-to-map-the-dark-universe/
- Published: 2026-08-31
- Topics: [Telescopes & Observatories](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/telescopes-and-observatories/); [Cosmology & Early Universe](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/cosmology-and-early-universe/); [Exoplanets](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/exoplanets/)
- Freshness context: NASA announced the launch on 30 August 2026.
- Summary: NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope launched on 30 August 2026 aboard a Falcon Heavy and is traveling to the Sun-Earth L2 point, about one million miles from Earth. Roman pairs a wide field with sharp infrared imaging to survey dark energy, dark matter, and exoplanets. Commissioning takes about three months. First public images are expected in early 2027.
- Why it matters: Roman is built for population questions: how cosmic expansion has changed, where dark matter sits, and how planets are distributed beyond the reach of transit surveys. Hubble and Webb cannot tile the sky this fast. The launch is real. The catalogues are not, until the images and the papers exist.
- Suggested next question: Look at gravitational microlensing, the brief brightening Roman will use to find planets on wide orbits and planets that orbit no star at all.
- Explore further: [NASA: the Roman Space Telescope launches](https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasas-dark-universe-seeking-nancy-grace-roman-space-telescope-launches/)
- Sources:
  - [NASA](https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasas-dark-universe-seeking-nancy-grace-roman-space-telescope-launches/)
  - [NASA JPL](https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/nasas-dark-universe-seeking-nancy-grace-roman-space-telescope-launches/)

Fuller note:

## Off the pad, and not yet taking data

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope launched at 7:26 a.m. EDT on 30 August 2026. A SpaceX Falcon Heavy carried it from Launch Complex 39A at Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The rocket separated from the observatory 31 minutes into the flight. After separating from the center core, the boosters returned to the launch site for refurbishment. Ground controllers at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center began receiving telemetry seven minutes after liftoff. An hour and 23 minutes after launch, the team confirmed that the solar panels and the lower instrument sun shade had deployed.

Roman is headed for the Sun-Earth L2 point, about one million miles from Earth. L2 is a parking region where the combined pull of the Sun and Earth lets a spacecraft keep pace with Earth as both travel around the Sun. The flight plan moves communications to the Deep Space Network about 70 minutes after launch: Canberra in Australia first, Madrid about six hours later, then Goldstone in California.

NASA describes a journey of about three months. Commissioning fills that same stretch: calibrations and tests, not science yet. First public images are expected in early 2027. Until those images exist, anything said about Roman's discoveries is a plan.

Within days of the announcement, the high-gain antenna and a visor-like aperture cover were still due to deploy, the first of two mid-course corrections was still ahead, and the Coronagraph Instrument was still due to power on. A few weeks into the voyage, the main camera, the Wide Field Instrument, was due to switch on. Those steps were the schedule in the launch release, not a stack of finished science.

## A wide infrared camera, and a mask for planets

The Wide Field Instrument is a 300-megapixel infrared camera with 18 detectors, each a 4K chip about the size of a saltine cracker. The telescope is built rigid and optically stable so it can move from one patch of sky to the next without a long settle. NASA says it is designed to survey the universe a thousand times faster than Hubble.

Roman's stated design pairs infrared sensitivity and image sharpness comparable to Hubble with a field of view roughly 100 times larger. A wide field is the point of a survey telescope. Hubble can stare hard at one patch. It cannot cheaply tile the sky. Roman is built to tile. It is expected to send back 1.4 terabytes of data a day, the highest rate of any NASA astrophysics mission so far. Machine learning, artificial intelligence, and citizen scientists are part of the plan for sorting that stream.

The coronagraph is a separate instrument. It blocks the glare of a star so a planet beside it can be photographed. On Roman it is a technology demonstration. NASA says it will take pictures of Jupiter-like planets, and that the same technique is one a future mission such as the Habitable Worlds Observatory concept could use when searching for Earth-like worlds. This flight is meant to show the method.

## Three surveys that have not started

NASA's main science goals are three population questions.

One is dark energy, the name for whatever is speeding up the expansion of the universe. A survey does not finish that question. It measures distances and the growth of structure across a large sample so competing descriptions can be told apart.

Another is dark matter, mapped through gravitational lensing. Mass bends light. With sharp images over a huge area, small distortions in the shapes of distant galaxies can be averaged into a map of the mass that did the bending, including mass that does not shine. That sentence is the method. Roman has not delivered the map.

The third is exoplanets, in the thousands, if the surveys work. A wide infrared campaign can catch many transits, the brief dips when a planet crosses its star. It can also watch for microlensing: a short brightening of a background star when a foreground star or planet passes almost in front and its gravity focuses the light. Microlensing is how you find worlds on wide orbits, and planets that are not orbiting a star at all. Transit surveys are good at close-in planets. They are poor at the ones far out. Roman's planet haul, if the survey performs, should look different from a Kepler-style catalogue because the method is different.

That reading is an interpretation of a survey that has not begun. The launch is the fact. The shape of the future catalogue is a forecast.

## Who built it, and what would count later

Julie McEnery, Roman's senior project scientist at Goddard, has said we have not had this kind of view before. Nicky Fox, at NASA's Science Mission Directorate, points to the large field of view and the fast survey speed. Administrator Jared Isaacman noted that the observatory was delivered ahead of schedule and on budget after more than a decade of work. Earlier in 2026, NASA and SpaceX moved the launch earlier because the telescope was finished ahead of the old date. Roman is the fourth primary NASA mission launched on a Falcon Heavy.

Goddard manages the telescope, with the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Caltech/IPAC, and the Space Telescope Science Institute. Industrial partners include BAE Systems, L3Harris Technologies, and Teledyne Scientific & Imaging. ESA, JAXA, the French space agency CNES, and the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy in Germany also contributed.

Dark energy, dark matter maps, and exoplanet counts need many objects measured the same way. That is why the launch matters before a single science image exists. The NASA release, and the JPL version of the same announcement, are the authority for the timeline and the stated goals. Papers that use Roman data do not exist yet.

### Earth may have slipped outside the Sun's protective bubble

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/earth-heliosphere/
- Published: 2026-08-30
- Topics: [Sun & Space Weather](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/sun-and-space-weather/); [Astrobiology & Habitability](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/astrobiology-and-habitability/)
- Freshness context: Highlighted by NASA on 24 August 2026. The review was published on 21 August 2026.
- Summary: Simulations from NASA's SHIELD center follow the Sun through the Milky Way and find dense interstellar clouds at about 2 to 3, 6 to 7, and 13 to 14 million years ago. Each time, the heliosphere, the bubble blown by the solar wind, may have shrunk inside Earth's orbit. Elements common in interstellar dust show up in ocean cores, Antarctic snow, and lunar samples on those dates.
- Why it matters: Earth's long-term environment depends on its orbit and on the Sun's activity, and also on where the Sun is traveling in the Galaxy. A smaller heliosphere would change the radiation and gas reaching the atmosphere. That adds an outside variable to climate and habitability in the geologically recent past.
- Suggested next question: Follow how the heliosphere changes size as the Sun moves through denser interstellar gas, and which measurements mark the edge of that bubble.
- Explore further: [NASA: how the Sun's path may have shaped Earth](https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/starstruck-nasa-research-shows-how-suns-ancient-history-shaped-earth/)
- Sources:
  - [NASA Science](https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/starstruck-nasa-research-shows-how-suns-ancient-history-shaped-earth/)
  - [Annual Reviews](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-astro-120425-053711)

Fuller note:

## A bubble that can be pressed inside Earth's orbit

The heliosphere is the bubble the solar wind blows in the gas between the stars. The solar wind is a stream of charged particles leaving the Sun in every direction. The bubble is not a hard wall. It is the region where that outflow still dominates. In ordinary times Earth sits well inside it. Spacecraft have crossed the boundary, so the edge is a place instruments have sampled, not a line that exists only on a diagram.

The Sun has been on the move for its whole life, about 4.6 billion years, carrying that bubble around the Milky Way. NASA's SHIELD center reconstructed a recent stretch of the path. SHIELD stands for Solar Wind with Hydrogen Ion charge Exchange and Large-Scale Dynamics. It is one of NASA's DRIVE science centers, led by Merav Opher at Boston University. The work is a review in the August 2026 volume of Annual Review of Astronomy and Astrophysics, published on 21 August 2026. NASA highlighted it on 24 August 2026.

In the simulations, the Sun ran into dense, cold interstellar clouds at least three times. The exposures fall at about 2 to 3 million years ago, 6 to 7 million years ago, and 13 to 14 million years ago. Each time, the cloud pressed the heliosphere down to smaller than Earth's orbit. Earth would have stayed bound to the Sun and left the solar-wind bubble, sitting for a while in interstellar space.

## Dust that shows up on the same dates

A cloud that compresses the heliosphere can also deliver dust. Elements common in interstellar dust show up in deep-sea sediment cores, Antarctic snow, and lunar samples on those same timelines. The match is why the encounters are more than a trajectory drawn through a map of the local Galaxy. The archives of the dust are mud, ice, and the Moon.

Keep the ranks straight. The simulated path, the three compressions, and the matching elements in those samples are the findings being reported. Opher's group built the heliosphere model as a digital twin, a computer copy meant to show how the bubble responds when the neighbourhood gets dense. The twin is a tool. The clouds and the dates are the output being compared with geology.

## Climate is a further step

Outside the bubble, galactic cosmic rays reach the atmosphere more easily, and the mix of incoming gas changes. Over the last tens of millions of years, Earth's climate has swung hard, including ice ages in which the global average temperature dropped by several degrees, with more frequent warm and cool spells inside those intervals. The usual explanations look inward: changes in Earth's orbit, greenhouse gases, and ice itself.

The SHIELD simulations follow a cold, dense galactic hydrogen cloud into the upper atmosphere. Water vapor increases. The dynamics aloft shift. From there, conditions at the surface can change. NASA's feature offers those exposures as a candidate external driver of ancient climate swings, including possible ice ages.

That reading is an interpretation. A specific ice age caused by a specific cloud is a further claim, past the trajectory and the dust elements. The group is arguing that the Sun's path through the Galaxy belongs in the climate conversation, alongside orbital cycles, greenhouse gases, and ice.

## A different paper on the same NASA page

The NASA feature also describes a separate study, and it should not be merged into the cloud result. Vladimir Airapetian, at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, looked at the faint young Sun. Three billion years ago the Sun was 70 percent as bright as it is today. Under that dimmer lamp Earth should have been frozen. Geological evidence shows liquid water was already here. The mismatch is called the faint young Sun paradox.

Young Sun-like stars observed by NASA's retired Kepler telescope throw off superflares, sending high-energy particles out on a daily basis. Airapetian's team put an early-Earth gas mix in a sealed chamber: molecular nitrogen, ammonia, carbon dioxide, and carbon monoxide. They fired protons into it. The bombardment produced nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas the feature describes as 300 times more potent than carbon dioxide. The paper is in Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Ultraviolet light from the young Sun would break some of that nitrous oxide back into nitrogen and oxygen. The team's simulations say that if only 10 percent survived, equatorial regions would still warm to about 41 degrees Fahrenheit, 5 degrees Celsius, above water's freezing point. The feature also notes that just-above-freezing temperatures have been found to be more efficient for building complex chains of amino acids than warmer temperatures. That warming story is their proposal for a different epoch. It is not the cold-cloud result, and it is not evidence for the three compressions.

The Annual Review article is the authority for the recent trajectory and the heliosphere model. NASA's write-up is the public account of both studies. The next object worth understanding is the heliosphere itself: how far the solar wind reaches, and how fast that reach collapses when a cold cloud arrives.

### Hubble identifies the Milky Way's earliest confirmed major merger

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/milky-way-earliest-major-merger/
- Published: 2026-08-29
- Topics: [Galaxies & Galactic Evolution](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/galaxies-and-galactic-evolution/)
- Freshness context: Published by NASA Hubble on 17 August 2026.
- Summary: Hubble ages and metallicities for 39 globular clusters in the inner Milky Way point to a dwarf galaxy, LKH, that merged with the Galaxy about 11.8 billion years ago. NASA's account puts that dwarf at roughly 500 million solar masses in stars and says the result pushes the confirmed merger record 1.8 billion years farther back. Stars born elsewhere were already part of the earliest growth.
- Why it matters: The Milky Way's confirmed merger history now reaches about 11.8 billion years back, 1.8 billion years earlier than the previous secure mark. The clusters say stars collected from outside were already part of the Galaxy's first growth, rather than a late addition after the disk was in place.
- Suggested next question: Look at how globular cluster ages and metallicities, paired with Gaia motions, separate stars born in the Milky Way from stars brought in by mergers.
- Explore further: [NASA Hubble: the Milky Way's earliest major merger](https://science.nasa.gov/missions/hubble/hubble-solves-merger-mystery-from-milky-ways-early-years/)
- Sources:
  - [NASA Hubble](https://science.nasa.gov/missions/hubble/hubble-solves-merger-mystery-from-milky-ways-early-years/)

Fuller note:

## A dwarf galaxy, eaten while the Milky Way was still small

About 11.8 billion years ago, a dwarf galaxy collided with the young Milky Way and merged with it. NASA's Hubble account, posted in August 2026, calls that the earliest confirmed major merger in the Galaxy's history. The date sits about two billion years after the Big Bang. The illustration that leads the article rounds the same collision to about 12 billion years ago. The finding pushes the confirmed merger record 1.8 billion years farther back than before.

The Milky Way today holds hundreds of billions of stars. It did not start that way. It grew by forming new stars from its own gas, and by taking stars, gas, and dark matter from smaller galaxies. The most recent massive case is the Sagittarius dwarf. That merger began more than 6 billion years ago and is still going. Earlier, the Galaxy consumed a dwarf called Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus about 10 billion years ago. That event rearranged a lot of the stellar disk. Smaller mergers sit between those two. Both observations and simulations had pointed at yet another large merger, earlier still. The arguments were about which clusters, which stars, and whether the evidence had been scrambled away. When the Milky Way was young it was smaller, closer in size to the galaxies it hit, and more chaotic. Signs of a merger can fade over billions of years.

Davide Massari, at the Astrophysics and Space Science Observatory of Bologna, led the work. His line on the result is domestic: we live in the Milky Way, and this paper asks where the first significant batch of bricks came from. The dwarf now has a name, LKH.

## Globular clusters as the archive

The team used Hubble to study globular clusters in the inner 20,000 light-years of the Galaxy. A globular cluster is a dense, roughly spherical ball of old stars, anywhere from tens of thousands of stars to a few million. The stars in one cluster share an age and a metallicity, the proportion of elements heavier than helium. That shared chemistry is why a cluster can act as a label from the galaxy where it formed, long after the parent galaxy is gone.

They looked at 39 clusters. Gaia, the European Space Agency mission that measures stellar motions, supplied the other axis. Chiara Zerbinati, a co-author at the University of Bologna, notes that Hubble's resolution and depth made the ages and metallicities precise enough to sort populations that blur together in less sharp data. The team expected two groups: clusters born in the young Milky Way, and clusters brought in by Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus about 10 billion years ago.

The sample split three ways. A third population is older than the Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus clusters and younger than the clusters born in the Milky Way, across the range of metallicity. Age and chemistry together are hard to produce inside one galaxy. They fit clusters born in a separate dwarf and delivered when that dwarf was eaten.

## The mass, and a name stitched from three papers

In NASA's account, the dwarf held roughly 500 million times the mass of the Sun in stars. That was a serious fraction of the Milky Way's mass at the time, which is why the merger counts as major. The Galaxy was smaller then. A partner of that size is not a light addition.

They named it Low-energy-Kraken-Heracles, LKH for short, after three earlier papers that had argued for an ancient merger without agreeing on the details. The compound name is a hint. Pieces of this galaxy were already in the literature. What was missing was a single object with a clock: when it fell in, and how massive it was. The 11.8 billion year date, set against the Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus merger at 10 billion years, is where the 1.8 billion years comes from. The paper reporting the cluster ages and the population split is in Nature Astronomy.

That reading is an interpretation of how the three cluster groups line up with three birthplaces. The measurements are the ages, the metallicities, and the motions. The assignment of the third group to one eaten dwarf is the team's conclusion from that pattern.

## What "confirmed" changes

Massari aims the result at a specific earlier claim: that the earliest Milky Way was built only from stars born in place. The LKH clusters say stars born in external galaxies were already part of that first growth. Accreted, here, means collected from outside rather than formed in the Milky Way's own gas. Fernando Aguado-Agelet, a co-author at the University of Vigo and the University of La Laguna, frames the follow-up as more clusters, including ones Hubble has not studied, so later mergers can be put on the same footing.

Confirmed does not mean the whole merger tree is finished. It means this event, at this time, with this mass in stars, is no longer only a disputed peak in a simulation or a chemical overdensity. The 1.8 billion years is a comparison with the previous confirmed milestone, not a claim that nothing happened before LKH. Earlier, smaller accretions can still be hiding in a record that the young Galaxy was quite capable of scrambling.

NASA's Hubble release is the public account. Nature Astronomy is the authority for the ages and the split. The useful next object is the globular cluster itself: a ball of stars that kept an age and a metal content while the galaxy around it was rebuilt.

### S301 may let astronomers measure the spin of Sagittarius A*

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/s301-sagittarius-a-star-spin/
- Published: 2026-08-28
- Topics: [Black Holes](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/black-holes/); [Gravity & Fundamental Physics](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/topics/gravity-and-fundamental-physics/)
- Freshness context: ESO announced the result on 19 August 2026. The paper is in Nature.
- Summary: S301 is the fastest known star in the Milky Way. At its closest approach to Sagittarius A*, it moves at about 25,000 kilometres per second, a bit over 8 percent of light speed, on an 8.7-year orbit that comes in near Saturn's distance. ESO reported the star on 19 August 2026. Later close passes may show the black hole's spin. That spin has not been measured.
- Why it matters: A spinning black hole drags spacetime, and that drag should show up in the orbit of a star this close and this fast. S301 gives observers a practical target for the test. The spin itself has not been measured. The orbit is the new tool, and the number is still ahead.
- Suggested next question: Follow how GRAVITY+ on the Very Large Telescope Interferometer times stellar orbits at the Galactic Centre, and what the 2031 close pass could add to a spin measurement.
- Explore further: [ESO: S301 and the spin of Sagittarius A*](https://eso.org/public/news/eso2612/)
- Sources:
  - [ESO](https://eso.org/public/news/eso2612/)

Fuller note:

## A star on a very short leash

S301 is the fastest star known in the Milky Way. At its closest pass to Sagittarius A*, the black hole at the Galactic Centre, it moves at about 25,000 kilometres per second. That is a bit over 8 percent of the speed of light. The black hole holds about four million times the mass of the Sun. The orbit takes 8.7 years. Closest approach is about 12 times the Earth-Sun distance, 1.78 billion kilometres, only about 20 percent farther than Saturn's distance from the Sun. No other star yet observed comes in that tight.

ESO announced the orbit on 19 August 2026. The paper, from the GRAVITY+ collaboration, is in Nature. The observations used the Very Large Telescope Interferometer at Paranal. Four 8-metre telescopes combine their light so they act as one. An interferometer does that on purpose: the sharpness comes from the separation between the telescopes, not from any single mirror. The instrument is GRAVITY, now in an upgraded form called GRAVITY+. Frank Eisenhauer, the GRAVITY+ principal investigator, notes that no other observatory has four telescopes of that size working as a single interferometer. The star is about two billion times fainter than Betelgeuse. They first caught it in spring 2023, traced the orbit back to 2017, and found that the last close pass was early 2023. The next one is in 2031.

Speed, period, closest distance, and a detection history are in hand. The spin of the black hole is not among them.

## What a spin would do, if the orbit is known well enough

A spinning black hole drags spacetime around with it. The drag should shift the path of a nearby star, and the shift grows when the star is close and fast. Relativistic, in this setting, means the piece of Einstein's gravity that stays small around Earth and shows up when speeds are a noticeable fraction of light speed and the mass is packed into a black hole. S301 spends the inner part of its orbit in that regime. S2 and the other famous Galactic Centre stars were the previous best stars for measuring the same drag. They do not pass as close.

Felix Mang, a PhD student at the Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics and an author of the study, is attached to a hope that should stay a hope. Within about ten years, this star could yield the spin of Sagittarius A*. Stefan Gillessen, who led much of the work with him, calls that a direct spin measurement and a sharp test of general relativity. It has not been done. One orbit is not enough. The team wants at least two full, well-sampled orbits so the trajectory is known tightly enough to see a small twist.

Juan Osorno, at the Paris Observatory, puts the practical consequence in plain terms. Without this star, the same spin measurement from the older stars would take several more decades. Reinhard Genzel, whose group's long campaign of stellar orbits helped establish the black hole, calls S301 a new window on spacetime near Sagittarius A*. The window is the orbit. The number for the spin is still ahead.

That reading is an interpretation of what a well-sampled orbit ought to contain. The data in hand are the path, not the twist.

## A torn pair is a fit, not a sighting

Stars do not form this close to the black hole. Tides in that neighbourhood pull a gas cloud apart before it can collapse into a star, so the usual inference is that S301 arrived from farther out. ESO labels the arrival story as an inference. The orbit fits a binary that was torn apart: one star captured onto the tight ellipse, the companion kicked out fast enough that it may have left the Galaxy. "Likely" is the word in the release. It is a clean dynamical story. Nobody has reported the ejected partner.

Other ways of dropping a single star onto such an ellipse are harder to square with that hostile inner region, which is why the torn-binary picture is the one the release prefers. Preference is not a detection. The orbit can be matched by a disrupted pair. That match does not prove the pair existed.

## 2031 is the next real test

MICADO, an instrument for ESO's Extremely Large Telescope, is named alongside GRAVITY+ as the follow-up. The 2031 pericentre is the next time the relativistic effects are strongest. Pericentre is just the closest point on the orbit. Missing that pass would weaken the chance of seeing any spin signal. Catching it, together with the track before and after, is the actual experiment.

Until that analysis is published, any figure offered as the spin of Sagittarius A* did not come from S301. What is in hand is the star, the speed, the period, the closest distance, the instrument, and a route to a measurement the older stars were not going to deliver on a short clock. What is not in hand is the spin. ESO's release eso2612 is the public account. The Nature paper is the authority for the orbital fit. Those two lists should not be folded into each other.
